- *Vorrei un caffè, per favore.* (I'd like a coffee, please.)
- *Potresti aiutarmi?* (Could you help me?)
- *Dovrei studiare di più.* (I should study more.)
- *Mi piacerebbe vedere Venezia.* (I'd like to see Venice.)

grammarPoints.title: Imperative with pronouns: dimmi, fallo, non toccarlo
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** when you give an order to *tu*, *noi* or *voi*, the pronouns (*mi, ti, lo, la, gli, ci, ne*...) are joined to the end of the verb: *guardami* (look at me), *prendilo* (take it).

- *tu*: *aspetta + mi → aspettami*, *prendi + lo → prendilo*
- *noi*: *andiamo + ci → andiamoci* (let's go there)
- *voi*: *prendete + le → prendetele*
- reflexive verbs work the same way: *alzati!* (get up!), *lavatevi le mani!*

The short *tu* forms *da', di', fa', sta', va'* double the first letter of the pronoun:

| verb | + pronoun |
|---|---|
| *di'* (say) | *dimmi, dillo* |
| *da'* (give) | *dammi, dalle* |
| *fa'* (do) | *fallo, fammi* |
| *va'* (go) | *vacci* |

The exception is *gli*, which never doubles: *digli* (tell him), *dagli* (give him).

In the negative *tu* form (*non* + infinitive), the pronoun can be attached to the infinitive or go before it: *non toccarlo* or *non lo toccare* (don't touch it).

This lesson covers *tu, noi, voi*. The polite *Lei* form works differently and comes next.

**Watch out:** write it as one word, with the stress staying where it was: *prendilo* (PREN-di-lo), not *prendi lo*. And remember the double letter: *dimmi*, not *dimi*.

Examples:
- *Dimmi la verità.* (Tell me the truth.)
- *Il libro è sul tavolo: prendilo.* (The book is on the table: take it.)
- *Non toccarlo, è fragile!* (Don't touch it, it's fragile!)
- *Se vedi Marco, digli di chiamarmi.* (If you see Marco, tell him to call me.)

grammarPoints.title: Polite imperative: Scusi, Venga, Si accomodi
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** to tell or ask someone you address as *Lei* (a stranger, a customer, an older person) to do something, you use the polite imperative: *Scusi, Senta, Venga, Si accomodi*.

How to build it:
- **-are** verbs end in **-i**: *scusare → scusi*, *aspettare → aspetti*, *guardare → guardi*
- **-ere** and **-ire** verbs end in **-a**: *prendere → prenda*, *sentire → senta*, *finire → finisca*

Many verbs build it from the *io* form of the present: *vengo → venga*, *faccio → faccia*, *dico → dica*, *vado → vada*, *esco → esca*, *bevo → beva*.

A few are fully irregular:

| verb | Lei form |
|---|---|
| essere | *sia* |
| avere | *abbia* |
| dare | *dia* |
| stare | *stia* |
| sapere | *sappia* |

Pronouns go **before** the verb, never attached: *Mi dica* (tell me), *Si accomodi* (have a seat), *Lo prenda* (take it), *Non si preoccupi* (don't worry). For the negative, just put *non* in front: *Non aspetti.*

To a group, everyday Italian simply uses the *voi* imperative: *Scusate, venite pure.*

**Watch out:** the vowels look "swapped": *-are* verbs take *-i* and the others take *-a*. So it's *Scusi* (from *scusare*) and *Senta* (from *sentire*), not *Scusa* and *Senti*, which are the *tu* forms you'd use with a friend.

Examples:
- *Scusi, dov'è la stazione?* (Excuse me, where is the station?)
- *Prego, si accomodi.* (Please, have a seat.)
- *Mi dica, cosa desidera?* (Tell me, what would you like?)
- *Non si preoccupi, ci penso io.* (Don't worry, I'll take care of it.)

grammarPoints.title: Double pronouns: me lo, te la, glielo
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** when a verb has two pronouns, "to someone" plus "it/them", Italian puts the "to someone" pronoun first and changes its form: *me lo* (it to me), *te la* (it to you), *glielo* (it to him or her).

The indirect object (who receives: "to me, to you") comes first, then the direct object (the thing: *lo, la, li, le*) or *ne*.

- *mi, ti, ci, vi* change their *i* to *e*: **me, te, ce, ve**. So *me lo, te la, ce li, ve le, me ne*.
- *gli* and *le* (to him, to her) and *Le* (to you, formal) all become **glie-**, written as one word with the next pronoun: *glielo, gliela, glieli, gliele, gliene*.
- Reflexive *si* becomes *se*: *se lo mette* (he puts it on).
- *ci* (there) + *ne* becomes *ce ne*: *Ce ne sono tre.* (There are three of them.)

| to | + lo | + la | + li / le |
|---|---|---|---|
| me | *me lo* | *me la* | *me li / me le* |
| you | *te lo* | *te la* | *te li / te le* |
| him, her | *glielo* | *gliela* | *glieli / gliele* |
| us | *ce lo* | *ce la* | *ce li / ce le* |

They go before the conjugated verb, or are attached as one word to an infinitive or a *tu* imperative: *Devo dirtelo*, *Dammelo!*. In the passato prossimo, *lo* and *la* become *l'* before *ho, ha*..., and the participle agrees with the thing: *Te l'ho data* (the letter), *Me le ha date* (the keys).

**Watch out:** the order is the reverse of English "give it to me": Italian says *me lo* (to me, it). And *glielo* can mean "it to him" or "it to her"; the context tells you which.

Examples:
- *Mi presti la penna? Sì, te la presto.* (Will you lend me the pen? Yes, I'll lend it to you.)
- *Porto i fiori alla nonna: glieli porto oggi.* (I'm taking the flowers to Grandma: I'm taking them to her today.)
- *Quel libro è mio: dammelo!* (That book is mine: give it to me!)

grammarPoints.title: Relative pronouns: che and cui
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** *che* and *cui* join two sentences by referring back to a noun, like English "who", "which", "that". Use *che* on its own, and *cui* after a preposition (a little word like *con, di, a, in, per*).

**che** means who, which or that. It is the subject (who does the action) or the direct object (what the action is done to) of the second part:
- *Il ragazzo che parla con Anna è mio fratello.* (who is talking)
- *Il libro che mi hai regalato è bello.* (that you gave me)

**cui** comes after a preposition. The preposition is the one the verb normally takes:

| preposition + cui | meaning |
|---|---|
| *con cui* | with whom, with which |
| *di cui* | about which, of which |
| *a cui* | to whom |
| *in cui* | in which, where, when |
| *per cui* | for which, why |
| *da cui* | from whom |

So *parlare di* gives *il film di cui ti ho parlato*, *avere bisogno di* gives *le cose di cui ho bisogno*. For places, *dove* is also fine: *la città in cui vivo* or *la città dove vivo*.

*che* and *cui* never change for gender or number.

**Watch out:** English can drop "that" ("the book I read"); Italian never drops *che*: *il libro che ho letto*. And never put *che* after a preposition: say *la ragazza con cui esco*, not *con che*. English puts the preposition at the end ("the girl I go out with"); Italian moves it to the front.

Examples:
- *Il libro che leggo è bellissimo.* (The book I'm reading is wonderful.)
- *L'amica con cui vado in vacanza si chiama Sara.* (The friend I'm going on holiday with is called Sara.)
- *Il film di cui ti ho parlato è uscito.* (The film I told you about has come out.)

grammarPoints.title: More uses of ci: ci penso, ci credo, ci metto
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** besides "there", *ci* replaces *a* + a thing or an idea (*ci penso*, I think about it), and it appears in fixed expressions such as *ci vuole* (it takes) and *ci metto* (it takes me).

**1. ci = a + thing or idea**, after verbs that take *a*:
- *pensare a* → *Ci penso io.* (I'll take care of it.)
- *credere a* → *Non ci credo!* (I don't believe it!)
- *riuscire a* → *Non ci riesco.* (I can't manage it.)
- *provare a* → *Voglio provarci.* (I want to give it a try.)

**2. How long it takes**

| expression | agrees with | example |
|---|---|---|
| *volerci* (it takes) | the thing needed | *Ci vuole un'ora. Ci vogliono due ore.* |
| *metterci* (it takes someone) | the person | *Ci metto un'ora. Ci mettiamo due ore.* |

In the passato prossimo, *volerci* uses *essere* (*Ci è voluta un'ora*) and *metterci* uses *avere* (*Ci ho messo un'ora*).

**3. Fixed expressions with senses:** *Non ci vedo* (I can't see), *Non ci sento* (I can't hear).

*ci* follows the usual pronoun position: before the conjugated verb, or attached to an infinitive.

**Watch out:** don't mix up *volerci* and *metterci*. *Ci vuole / ci vogliono* changes with the time or thing (*ci vogliono tre ore*), and has no person. *Metterci* changes with the person who takes the time: *ci metto, ci metti, ci mette*. English "it takes me an hour" is most simply *ci metto un'ora*.

Examples:
- *Non preoccuparti, ci penso io.* (Don't worry, I'll take care of it.)
- *Per arrivare a Roma ci vogliono tre ore.* (It takes three hours to get to Rome.)
- *Quanto ci metti per andare al lavoro?* (How long does it take you to get to work?)

grammarPoints.title: More uses of ne: ne parlo, ne ho mangiati tre
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** *ne* also replaces *di* + something ("about it", "of it"), and in the passato prossimo with a quantity the participle agrees with the thing counted: *Ne ho mangiati tre* (biscuits).

**1. ne = di + something**, after verbs and expressions that take *di*:
- *parlare di* → *Ne parliamo domani.* (We'll talk about it tomorrow.)
- *avere bisogno di* → *Ne ho bisogno.* (I need it.)
- *pensare di* (have an opinion) → *Che ne pensi?* (What do you think of it?)
- *essere contento / sicuro di* → *Ne sono sicuro.* (I'm sure of it.)
- *sapere di* → *Ne sai qualcosa?* (Do you know anything about it?)

**2. ne + quantity in the passato prossimo.** The participle takes the gender and number of the noun that *ne* replaces:

| noun replaced | sentence |
|---|---|
| *biscotti* (m. pl.) | *Ne ho mangiati tre.* |
| *birre* (f. pl.) | *Ne abbiamo bevute due.* |
| *lettera* (f. sing.) | *Ne ho scritta una.* |

When *ne* means "about it" (*di* + thing), there is no agreement: *Ne abbiamo parlato.*

A useful idiom: *Non ne posso più!* (I can't take any more!)

**Watch out:** English never changes the verb here, so it's easy to forget the agreement: *Quante foto hai fatto? Ne ho fatte cento*, with *-e* because *foto* is feminine plural. Look back at the noun to choose the ending.

Examples:
- *Che ne pensi di questo film?* (What do you think of this film?)
- *Quanti biscotti hai mangiato? Ne ho mangiati tre.* (How many biscuits did you eat? I ate three.)
- *Ne abbiamo parlato ieri.* (We talked about it yesterday.)

grammarPoints.title: Better and worse: migliore, meglio, peggiore, peggio
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** "better" and "worse" have two forms each in Italian. Use *migliore / peggiore* with a noun (a thing or person) and *meglio / peggio* with a verb.

| | goes with a noun (adjective) | goes with a verb (adverb) |
|---|---|---|
| better | *migliore* (pl. *migliori*) | *meglio* |
| worse | *peggiore* (pl. *peggiori*) | *peggio* |

- An adjective (a word that describes a noun) changes in the plural: *i ristoranti migliori*.
- An adverb (a word that describes how you do something) never changes: *Parli meglio di me.*
- With *stare* and *sentirsi* (how you feel) use the adverb: *Oggi sto meglio.*
- *È meglio* + infinitive means "it's better to": *È meglio partire presto.*

Add the article to say "the best, the worst": *il migliore*, *la peggiore*. Before a noun, *migliore* often shortens to *miglior*: *il mio miglior amico*.

Two more pairs:
- *maggiore / minore*: older / younger, for brothers and sisters (*mia sorella maggiore*)
- *ottimo / pessimo*: excellent / terrible, the strongest forms of *buono / cattivo*

For food, *più buono* is also common and correct: *Questa pizza è più buona.*

**Watch out:** "better" in English is one word, so learners say *Parli migliore* or *È una meglio idea*. Ask: does it describe a noun (*migliore*) or a verb (*meglio*)? And never say *più meglio*: *meglio* already means "more good".

Examples:
- *Questa pizza è migliore di quella di ieri.* (This pizza is better than yesterday's.)
- *Oggi sto meglio, grazie.* (I feel better today, thanks.)
- *Marco canta peggio di me.* (Marco sings worse than me.)
- *È stata la giornata peggiore della mia vita.* (It was the worst day of my life.)

grammarPoints.title: Past perfect: avevo già mangiato
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the trapassato prossimo is the Italian "had done". It describes something that happened before another moment in the past.

Build it like the passato prossimo, but put the auxiliary (*avere* or *essere*) in the imperfect:

| | mangiare (with avere) | partire (with essere) |
|---|---|---|
| io | *avevo mangiato* | *ero partito / partita* |
| tu | *avevi mangiato* | *eri partito / partita* |
| lui, lei | *aveva mangiato* | *era partito / partita* |
| noi | *avevamo mangiato* | *eravamo partiti / partite* |
| voi | *avevate mangiato* | *eravate partiti / partite* |
| loro | *avevano mangiato* | *erano partiti / partite* |

The same verbs take *essere* as in the passato prossimo (verbs of movement and change, reflexive verbs), and with *essere* the participle agrees with the subject: *Anna era uscita*, *si era sposata*.

You use it when you are already talking about the past and need to go one step further back:
- *Quando sono arrivato, il film era cominciato.* (The film started first, then I arrived.)
- *Non avevo fame perché avevo mangiato tardi.*

Words like *già* (already), *mai* (ever, never) and *appena* (just) go between the auxiliary and the participle: *era già partito*.

**Watch out:** English often uses the simple past where Italian needs this tense: "I realised I forgot my keys" is *Mi sono accorto che avevo dimenticato le chiavi*. If one past event clearly comes before another, use the trapassato for the earlier one.

Examples:
- *Quando sono arrivato, il treno era già partito.* (When I arrived, the train had already left.)
- *Non avevo mai visto il mare.* (I had never seen the sea.)
- *Anna era stanca perché aveva lavorato tutto il giorno.* (Anna was tired because she had worked all day.)

grammarPoints.title: Future perfect and guessing: avrò finito, sarà stanco
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the future perfect (*avrò finito*, I will have finished) says that something will be done before a moment in the future. Italian also uses the future tenses to make guesses: *sarà stanco* (he's probably tired), *avrà perso il treno* (he must have missed the train).

Build it with the future of *avere* or *essere* + the participle:

| | finire (with avere) | arrivare (with essere) |
|---|---|---|
| io | *avrò finito* | *sarò arrivato / arrivata* |
| tu | *avrai finito* | *sarai arrivato / arrivata* |
| lui, lei | *avrà finito* | *sarà arrivato / arrivata* |
| noi | *avremo finito* | *saremo arrivati / arrivate* |
| voi | *avrete finito* | *sarete arrivati / arrivate* |
| loro | *avranno finito* | *saranno arrivati / arrivate* |

**1. Finished before a future moment**, often after *quando, appena* (as soon as), *dopo che* or with *entro* (by):
- *Domani a quest'ora avrò finito l'esame.*
- *Ti chiamo appena sarò arrivato.*

**2. Guessing**
- about now: simple future. *Non risponde: sarà in riunione.* (He's probably in a meeting.)
- about the past: future perfect. *Marco non è qui: avrà perso il treno.* (He must have missed the train.)
- wondering: *Dove avrò messo gli occhiali?* (Where can I have put my glasses?)

**Watch out:** in a guess the future does not talk about the future at all. *Saranno le tre* means "it must be about three o'clock" right now. Use the simple future for a guess about the present and the future perfect for a guess about something already done.

Examples:
- *Quando avremo finito i lavori, faremo una festa.* (When we've finished the work, we'll have a party.)
- *Che ore sono? Saranno le tre.* (What time is it? It must be about three.)
- *Le luci sono spente: saranno usciti.* (The lights are off: they must have gone out.)

grammarPoints.title: Past conditional: avrei voluto, sarei venuto
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the past conditional is "would have done": *avrei voluto* (I would have liked), *sarei venuto* (I would have come). It is also how Italian says "would" when reporting a past promise: *Ha detto che sarebbe venuto.*

Build it with the conditional of *avere* or *essere* + the participle:

| | volere (with avere) | venire (with essere) |
|---|---|---|
| io | *avrei voluto* | *sarei venuto / venuta* |
| tu | *avresti voluto* | *saresti venuto / venuta* |
| lui, lei | *avrebbe voluto* | *sarebbe venuto / venuta* |
| noi | *avremmo voluto* | *saremmo venuti / venute* |
| voi | *avreste voluto* | *sareste venuti / venute* |
| loro | *avrebbero voluto* | *sarebbero venuti / venute* |

The main uses:
- something that didn't happen: *Avrei comprato quella giacca, ma costava troppo.*
- regrets and criticism with modal verbs: *avrei dovuto* (I should have), *avrei potuto* (I could have): *Avresti dovuto dirmelo!*
- **the future seen from the past**, after a past verb like *ha detto, pensavo, sapevo*: *Marco ha detto che sarebbe arrivato alle otto.* (Marco said he would arrive at eight.)

**Watch out:** in that last use English has a simple "would" ("he said he would come"), so learners use the present conditional: *ha detto che verrebbe*. That is wrong in standard Italian. After a past verb of saying or thinking, use the past conditional: *ha detto che sarebbe venuto*, even if he may still come.

Examples:
- *Avrei voluto venire, ma ero malato.* (I would have liked to come, but I was ill.)
- *Avresti dovuto dirmelo prima!* (You should have told me before!)
- *Pensavo che il film sarebbe stato noioso.* (I thought the film would be boring.)

grammarPoints.title: Impersonal si: si mangia bene qui
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** *si* + a verb in the *lui/lei* form talks about people in general, like English "you", "one", "people" or "they": *Qui si mangia bene.* (You eat well here.)

How it works:
- *si* + third person singular: *si mangia, si dice, si parte, si arriva*.
- In the negative: *non si* + verb: *Qui non si fuma.*
- With a plural noun (the thing people buy, sell, eat...), the verb goes plural: *Qui si vendono biglietti.* More on this in a later lesson.
- With *essere*, an adjective after it is plural: *Quando si è giovani...*
- With a reflexive verb (*alzarsi, vestirsi*), you can't say *si si*: it becomes **ci si**: *In vacanza ci si alza tardi.*
- In the passato prossimo it uses *essere*: *Alla festa si è ballato molto.*

| personal | impersonal |
|---|---|
| *Mangio bene qui.* (I eat well) | *Si mangia bene qui.* (you eat well) |
| *Come dici "grazie"?* | *Come si dice "grazie"?* |
| *Mi alzo tardi.* | *Ci si alza tardi.* |

**Watch out:** English uses "you" or "they" for people in general; don't translate them as *tu* or *loro*. "How do you say...?" is *Come si dice...?*, and "they speak Italian here" is *Qui si parla italiano*.

Examples:
- *In questo ristorante si mangia benissimo.* (You eat really well in this restaurant.)
- *Come si dice "thank you" in italiano?* (How do you say "thank you" in Italian?)
- *In vacanza ci si alza tardi.* (On holiday you get up late.)

grammarPoints.title: Bisogna, basta, serve, conviene
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** some very common verbs have no real subject (no "I", "you" or "he" doing the action). They say what is necessary, enough, needed or worth doing: *bisogna, basta, serve, conviene*.

| verb | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *bisogna* + infinitive | you have to, it's necessary | *Bisogna avere il biglietto.* |
| *basta* + infinitive or noun | you only need, it's enough | *Basta chiedere.* *Basta un minuto.* |
| *serve / servono* | is / are needed | *Mi serve una penna.* |
| *conviene* + infinitive | it's better, it's worth it | *Ti conviene prendere il treno.* |

- **bisogna** never changes and takes no pronoun. To say "I need something", use *ho bisogno di*.
- **basta** on its own means "Enough!", and *Basta con...!* means "Enough of...!"
- **servire** works like *piacere*: the person goes in an indirect pronoun (*mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi*) or with *a*, and the verb agrees with the thing needed: *Mi serve la macchina*, *Mi servono due uova*. In the passato prossimo it uses *essere*: *Il tuo aiuto mi è servito.*
- **conviene** also takes the indirect pronoun for the person: *Ci conviene partire presto.* (We'd better leave early.)

**Watch out:** with *servire*, the thing needed is the subject, as with *piacere*. So it's *Mi servono le chiavi* (plural, because of *le chiavi*), not *Mi serve le chiavi* and not *Io servo le chiavi*.

Examples:
- *Per entrare bisogna avere il biglietto.* (You need a ticket to get in.)
- *Basta chiedere al bancone.* (You just need to ask at the counter.)
- *Per la torta mi servono tre uova.* (I need three eggs for the cake.)
- *Ti conviene prendere la metro.* (You'd better take the underground.)

grammarPoints.title: About to: stare per + infinitive
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** *stare per* + infinitive means "to be about to" do something: *Sto per uscire.* (I'm about to go out.)

Use *stare* in the present for now, and in the imperfect for the past:

| | present | imperfect |
|---|---|---|
| io | *sto per uscire* | *stavo per uscire* |
| tu | *stai per uscire* | *stavi per uscire* |
| lui, lei | *sta per uscire* | *stava per uscire* |
| noi | *stiamo per uscire* | *stavamo per uscire* |
| voi | *state per uscire* | *stavate per uscire* |
| loro | *stanno per uscire* | *stavano per uscire* |

- The infinitive never changes; only *stare* changes for the person.
- Pronouns attach to the infinitive: *Stavo per chiamarti.* (I was just about to call you.)
- The imperfect is very common when something interrupts the action, or when it nearly happened: *Stavo per dimenticare il portafoglio.* (I nearly forgot my wallet.)
- It works with weather too: *Sta per piovere.*

**Watch out:** don't confuse it with *stare* + gerund (the *-ando, -endo* form), which you learnt earlier. *Sto mangiando* means "I'm eating" right now; *Sto per mangiare* means "I'm about to eat". And don't translate "about" literally: *sono circa di uscire* is wrong.

Examples:
- *Aspetta, sto per uscire.* (Wait, I'm about to go out.)
- *Il treno sta per partire.* (The train is about to leave.)
- *Quando hai telefonato, stavamo per mangiare.* (When you rang, we were about to eat.)

grammarPoints.title: Gerund clauses: studiando, ho imparato
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** The gerund (the *-ando, -endo* form you know from *sto parlando*) can stand on its own to say **how**, **when**, **why** or **on what condition** something happens. It replaces a whole clause (a part of the sentence with its own verb).

Forms: *-are* verbs take *-ando* (*parlando*), *-ere* and *-ire* verbs take *-endo* (*prendendo, partendo*). Irregular ones use the long stem: *facendo, dicendo, bevendo*.

What it can mean:
- how, by what means: *Studiando ogni giorno, ho imparato.* (By studying every day, I learnt.)
- while, when: *Tornando a casa, ho incontrato Luca.* (On my way home, I ran into Luca.)
- why, since: *Essendo stanca, sono andata a letto.* (Being tired, I went to bed.)
- if: *Volendo, possiamo partire domani.* (If we want, we can leave tomorrow.)
- although, with *pur*: *Pur avendo poco tempo, mi ha aiutato.* (Although he had little time, he helped me.)

Object pronouns attach to the end: *vedendola* (seeing her), *parlandogli* (talking to him).

The gerund normally has the same subject as the main verb. *Uscendo, ho visto Anna* means I was going out, not Anna.

**Watch out:** many English "-ing" forms are not gerunds in Italian. After a preposition, or as a subject, use the infinitive: "before leaving" is *prima di partire*, "without saying" is *senza dire*, "swimming is good for you" is *nuotare fa bene*.

Examples:
- *Sbagliando s'impara.* (You learn by making mistakes.)
- *Leggendo il giornale, ho scoperto la notizia.* (Reading the newspaper, I found out the news.)
- *Il bambino è entrato piangendo.* (The child came in crying.)

grammarPoints.title: Before and after: prima di + infinitive, dopo aver fatto
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** to say "before doing" use *prima di* + infinitive (*prima di mangiare*). To say "after doing" use *dopo* + the past infinitive (*dopo aver mangiato*).

**Before:** *prima di* + infinitive.
- *Lavati le mani prima di mangiare.* (before eating)
- Pronouns attach to the infinitive: *prima di vederti*, *prima di alzarsi*.

**After:** *dopo* + past infinitive. The past infinitive is *avere* or *essere* + the participle:
- with *avere* (usually shortened to *aver*): *dopo aver mangiato, dopo aver finito*
- with *essere*, the participle agrees with the subject: *dopo essere arrivato / arrivata / arrivati / arrivate*
- reflexive verbs attach the pronoun to *essere*: *dopo essermi alzato, dopo essersi alzata*

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| mangiare | *prima di mangiare* | *dopo aver mangiato* |
| uscire | *prima di uscire* | *dopo essere uscito/a* |
| alzarsi | *prima di alzarsi* | *dopo essersi alzato/a* |

The past infinitive is also used after *grazie per* (thanks for): *Grazie per essere venuti!*

Both work only when the person doing the two actions is the same: *Dopo aver mangiato (io), sono uscito (io).*

**Watch out:** English uses the *-ing* form ("before eating, after leaving"), but Italian never uses the gerund here. Say *prima di partire*, not *prima partendo*. For "after", the simple infinitive is a common mistake: say *dopo aver mangiato*, not *dopo mangiare*.

Examples:
- *Chiamami prima di partire.* (Call me before you leave.)
- *Dopo aver finito il lavoro, sono andato in palestra.* (After finishing work, I went to the gym.)
- *Dopo essere arrivata a casa, Anna ha fatto una doccia.* (After getting home, Anna had a shower.)

grammarPoints.title: Linking ideas: quindi, però, invece, siccome, anche se
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** connectors are the small words that link ideas and show how they relate: a result, a contrast, a reason. They make your Italian sound fluent instead of a list of short sentences.

| connector | meaning | use |
|---|---|---|
| *quindi, allora* | so, therefore | a result |
| *però* | but, however | a contrast |
| *invece* | instead, whereas, on the other hand | a different choice or a comparison |
| *siccome* | since, as | a reason, at the start of the sentence |
| *perché* | because | a reason, after the main idea |
| *anche se* | even though, even if | a contrast with a fact |
| *mentre* | while | two things at the same time |
| *infatti* | indeed, and sure enough | confirms what was just said |
| *comunque* | anyway, however | moving on despite something |

A few notes on position:
- *siccome* comes first: *Siccome era tardi, abbiamo preso un taxi.* With the reason second, use *perché*: *Abbiamo preso un taxi perché era tardi.*
- *però* and *invece* can also go after the subject or at the end: *Io prendo il treno, Marco invece va in macchina.*
- *comunque* can go at the end too: *Esco comunque.* (I'm going out anyway.)
- *anche se* takes the normal indicative (the ordinary present, past...): *Esco anche se piove.*

**Watch out:** *infatti* is a false friend. It doesn't correct anything like English "in fact" ("I thought it was easy; in fact, it was hard"). It confirms: *Ha detto che sarebbe arrivato tardi, e infatti è arrivato alle dieci.* To correct, use *invece* or *in realtà*.

Examples:
- *Piove, quindi restiamo a casa.* (It's raining, so we're staying in.)
- *Il ristorante è caro, però si mangia bene.* (The restaurant is expensive, but the food is good.)
- *Siccome era tardi, abbiamo preso un taxi.* (As it was late, we took a taxi.)
- *Esco anche se piove.* (I'm going out even though it's raining.)

grammarPoints.title: Real conditions: se + present or future
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** to talk about something that can really happen ("if it rains, we'll stay in"), use *se* (if) + the present or the future, and the present, future or imperative in the other part.

A sentence with *se* has two parts: the condition (*se piove*) and the result (*restiamo a casa*).

| condition (se...) | result |
|---|---|
| present: *Se piove,* | present: *restiamo a casa.* |
| present: *Se hai fame,* | imperative: *mangia qualcosa!* |
| future: *Se avrò tempo,* | future: *ti chiamerò.* |

- In everyday speech the present in both parts is the most common: *Se vuoi, ti accompagno.*
- When the whole thing is in the future, you can use the future in both parts, which sounds a little more careful: *Se domani farà bel tempo, andremo al mare.*
- The order can change: *Ti chiamo se arrivo tardi.*

These are real, possible conditions. For imaginary ones ("if I were rich") Italian uses other tenses, which come later.

**Watch out:** English never puts "will" after "if", but Italian can use the future there: *Se verrai, sarò contento* is correct. The opposite mistake is worse: don't use the conditional for a real condition. "If you want, I'll help you" is *Se vuoi, ti aiuto*, not *Se vuoi, ti aiuterei*.

Examples:
- *Se piove, restiamo a casa.* (If it rains, we'll stay in.)
- *Se vuoi, ti accompagno io.* (If you like, I'll take you.)
- *Se avrò tempo, ti chiamerò.* (If I have time, I'll call you.)
- *Se ti senti male, chiama il medico.* (If you feel ill, call the doctor.)

grammarPoints.title: The passive with essere: è stato costruito
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** In a passive sentence the thing that receives the action becomes the subject: "the house was built" instead of "they built the house". Italian forms it with **essere + past participle**, and the participle agrees with the subject like an adjective.

How to build it: put *essere* in the tense you need, then add the participle.

| Tense | Passive |
|---|---|
| present | *è costruito* (is built) |
| imperfetto | *era costruito* (was built, used to be) |
| passato prossimo | *è stato costruito* (was built, has been built) |
| future | *sarà costruito* (will be built) |

In compound tenses both *stato* and the participle agree: *la casa è stata venduta*, *i ponti sono stati costruiti*, *le lettere sono state scritte*.

To say who did it (the agent), use *da* (with its article: *dal, dalla, dai*...):
- *Il libro è stato scritto da Calvino.* (The book was written by Calvino.)
- *Il ladro è stato arrestato dalla polizia.* (The thief was arrested by the police.)

Only verbs that can take a direct object (a "what?" after the verb, like *vendere qualcosa*) can be made passive. *Andare* or *arrivare* cannot.

The passive works in every mood too: *Penso che il problema sia stato risolto.* (I think the problem has been solved.)

**Watch out:** "by" is *da*, never *per*: *scritto da Calvino*. And do not forget the double agreement: *la finestra è stata aperta*, not *è stato aperto*.

Examples:
- *Il Colosseo è stato costruito quasi duemila anni fa.* (The Colosseum was built almost two thousand years ago.)
- *Questi prodotti sono venduti in tutto il mondo.* (These products are sold all over the world.)
- *I risultati saranno pubblicati lunedì.* (The results will be published on Monday.)

grammarPoints.title: Present subjunctive: forms
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the subjunctive (*congiuntivo*) is a set of verb forms used after *che* when you express an opinion, a wish, a doubt or a feeling: *Penso che sia vero.* This lesson is about how to build the present subjunctive.

Regular verbs swap the typical vowel: *-are* verbs take **-i**, *-ere* and *-ire* verbs take **-a**:

| | parlare | prendere | partire |
|---|---|---|---|
| io, tu, lui | *parli* | *prenda* | *parta* |
| noi | *parliamo* | *prendiamo* | *partiamo* |
| voi | *parliate* | *prendiate* | *partiate* |
| loro | *parlino* | *prendano* | *partano* |

- The three singular forms are the same, so add *tu*, *lui*, *lei* when it's unclear: *Penso che tu abbia ragione.*
- The *noi* form is the same as the present: *parliamo*.
- *-isc-* verbs keep it: *finisca, capiscano*. Verbs in *-care, -gare* add *h*: *cerchi, paghi*.

Many verbs build it from the *io* present: *faccio → faccia*, *vado → vada*, *vengo → venga*, *dico → dica*, *posso → possa*, *voglio → voglia*, *devo → debba*, *esco → esca*. Their *noi* and *voi* forms are regular: *facciamo, andiate, veniate*.

Fully irregular:

| essere | avere | sapere | dare / stare |
|---|---|---|---|
| *sia, siano* | *abbia, abbiano* | *sappia, sappiano* | *dia / stia* |

The *noi* forms are *siamo, abbiamo, sappiamo, diamo, stiamo*, and the *voi* forms *siate, abbiate, sappiate, diate, stiate*.

**Watch out:** these endings look like the "wrong" conjugation: *parli* is not the *tu* present here, and *prenda* is not a mistake for *prende*. Think of the polite imperative (*Scusi, Prenda*): it uses exactly the same forms.

Examples:
- *Penso che Marco parli bene l'inglese.* (I think Marco speaks English well.)
- *Spero che tu stia bene.* (I hope you're well.)
- *Voglio che i bambini vadano a letto presto.* (I want the children to go to bed early.)

grammarPoints.title: Subjunctive after penso che, voglio che, spero che
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** after verbs of opinion, wish, hope, doubt or feeling followed by *che*, the second verb goes in the subjunctive: *Penso che sia tardi.* (I think it's late.)

The main triggers:
- **opinion:** *penso che, credo che, mi sembra che, immagino che*
- **wish or will:** *voglio che, preferisco che, desidero che*
- **hope and feelings:** *spero che, sono contento che, mi dispiace che, ho paura che*
- **doubt:** *dubito che, non credo che, non sono sicuro che*

The subjunctive is needed only when the two parts have **different subjects** (different people doing the actions). When the subject is the same, use *di* + infinitive (or just the infinitive after *voglio, preferisco*):

| different people | same person |
|---|---|
| *Spero che tu venga.* | *Spero di venire.* |
| *Voglio che tu parta.* | *Voglio partire.* |
| *Penso che lui abbia ragione.* | *Penso di avere ragione.* |

Certainty takes the ordinary indicative (the normal present, past, future): *So che hai ragione*, *Sono sicuro che viene*, *Secondo me è vero*.

**Watch out:** English says "I want you to come", so learners say *Voglio te venire*. Italian needs a *che* clause with the subjunctive: *Voglio che tu venga.* And with the same subject, don't use *che* at all: *Spero di vederti*, not *Spero che io ti veda*.

Examples:
- *Penso che Anna sia a casa.* (I think Anna is at home.)
- *Voglio che tu venga con me.* (I want you to come with me.)
- *Spero di vederti presto.* (I hope to see you soon.)
- *So che Marco ha ragione.* (I know Marco is right.)

grammarPoints.title: Subjunctive after è importante che, bisogna che
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** impersonal expressions (ones with no real "I" or "you", like "it is important that") take the subjunctive when they are followed by *che*: *È importante che tu dorma.*

Common expressions that take the subjunctive:
- necessity: *bisogna che, è necessario che, è ora che* (it's time that)
- judgement: *è importante che, è meglio che, è giusto che, è strano che, peccato che* (it's a shame that)
- possibility: *è possibile che, è probabile che, può darsi che* (maybe)
- condition: *basta che* (as long as)

When the sentence is about people in general, with no specific person, use the infinitive without *che*:

| general | about a specific person |
|---|---|
| *È importante dormire.* | *È importante che tu dorma.* |
| *Bisogna partire.* | *Bisogna che partiamo.* |
| *È meglio aspettare.* | *È meglio che aspettiate.* |

Expressions of certainty take the ordinary indicative: *è vero che, è chiaro che, è certo che, è evidente che*: *È vero che Luca vive a Londra.*

**Watch out:** *è vero che* and *è chiaro che* look like the other *è ... che* phrases, but they state a fact, so no subjunctive: *È chiaro che hai ragione*, not *abbia*. With *bisogna*, the infinitive is the everyday choice for general rules; use *bisogna che* + subjunctive only when you name who has to do it.

Examples:
- *È importante che tu dorma almeno otto ore.* (It's important that you sleep at least eight hours.)
- *Bisogna che voi arriviate in orario.* (You need to arrive on time.)
- *Peccato che tu non possa venire.* (It's a shame you can't come.)
- *È vero che Luca vive a Londra.* (It's true that Luca lives in London.)

grammarPoints.title: Past subjunctive: credo che sia partito
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the past subjunctive (*congiuntivo passato*) is used after *penso che, spero che, è possibile che* and the other triggers when the action has already happened: *Credo che sia partito ieri.* (I think he left yesterday.)

Build it like the passato prossimo, with the auxiliary in the present subjunctive: *abbia* or *sia* + the participle.

| | finire (with avere) | partire (with essere) |
|---|---|---|
| io, tu, lui, lei | *abbia finito* | *sia partito / partita* |
| noi | *abbiamo finito* | *siamo partiti / partite* |
| voi | *abbiate finito* | *siate partiti / partite* |
| loro | *abbiano finito* | *siano partiti / partite* |

The same verbs take *essere* as in the passato prossimo, and the participle agrees in the same way: *Spero che le ragazze siano tornate.* Reflexive verbs use *essere*: *Sono contenta che vi siate divertiti.*

Choose the tense by when the second action happens, compared with the first verb (here in the present):
- same time or later: present subjunctive. *Penso che parta.* (I think he's leaving.)
- earlier: past subjunctive. *Penso che sia partito.* (I think he has left / he left.)

As before, when the subject is the same, use *di* + the past infinitive: *Ho paura di aver sbagliato.* (I'm afraid I made a mistake.)

**Watch out:** English uses the same "I think he left" for many past events; Italian doesn't use the passato prossimo after these triggers. Say *Credo che sia partito*, not *Credo che è partito*. And remember the agreement with *essere*: *Credo che Giulia sia andata a casa.*

Examples:
- *Credo che Marco sia partito ieri.* (I think Marco left yesterday.)
- *Spero che tu abbia dormito bene.* (I hope you slept well.)
- *Mi dispiace che abbiate perso il treno.* (I'm sorry you missed the train.)

grammarPoints.title: Imperfect subjunctive: volevo che tu venissi
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** The imperfect subjunctive (*congiuntivo imperfetto*) is the past partner of the present subjunctive. You use it in the same kinds of sentences (wishes, opinions, doubts, feelings) when the main verb is in a past tense or in the conditional.

How to build it: take the imperfetto without *-vo* (*parla-vo*, *prende-vo*, *dormi-vo*) and add **-ssi, -ssi, -sse, -ssimo, -ste, -ssero**.

| | parlare | prendere | dormire |
|---|---|---|---|
| io | parlassi | prendessi | dormissi |
| tu | parlassi | prendessi | dormissi |
| lui, lei | parlasse | prendesse | dormisse |
| noi | parlassimo | prendessimo | dormissimo |
| voi | parlaste | prendeste | dormiste |
| loro | parlassero | prendessero | dormissero |

Verbs with a longer imperfetto stem keep it: *fare* gives *facessi*, *dire* gives *dicessi*, *bere* gives *bevessi*. *Avere* is regular: *avessi, avesse*.

The truly irregular ones:
- *essere*: fossi, fossi, fosse, fossimo, foste, fossero
- *dare*: dessi, dessi, desse, dessimo, deste, dessero
- *stare*: stessi, stessi, stesse, stessimo, steste, stessero

When to use it: the main verb is past or conditional and the action happens at the same time or later.
- *Penso che sia stanco.* becomes *Pensavo che fosse stanco.*
- *Vorrei che tu restassi.* (I'd like you to stay.)

**Watch out:** English says "I wanted you to come" with an infinitive. Italian needs *che* + subjunctive when the two people are different: *volevo che tu venissi*, never *volevo te venire*. Also, *io* and *tu* share one form, so add *tu* when the meaning is unclear.

Examples:
- *Volevo che tu venissi alla festa.* (I wanted you to come to the party.)
- *Pensavo che fosse italiano.* (I thought he was Italian.)
- *Vorrei che mi dicessi la verità.* (I'd like you to tell me the truth.)

grammarPoints.title: Pluperfect subjunctive: pensavo che fosse già partito
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** The pluperfect subjunctive (*congiuntivo trapassato*) means "had done" in a subjunctive sentence. Use it when the main verb is past or conditional and the other action happened **before** it.

How to build it: the imperfect subjunctive of *avere* or *essere* + the past participle (the *-ato, -uto, -ito* form). Choose *avere* or *essere* exactly as in the passato prossimo.

| | finire | uscire |
|---|---|---|
| io | avessi finito | fossi uscito/a |
| tu | avessi finito | fossi uscito/a |
| lui, lei | avesse finito | fosse uscito/a |
| noi | avessimo finito | fossimo usciti/e |
| voi | aveste finito | foste usciti/e |
| loro | avessero finito | fossero usciti/e |

With *essere*, the participle agrees with the subject (who does the action): *-o, -a, -i, -e*.

Pick the tense by timing:
- *Pensavo che mangiasse.* (I thought he was eating: same time.)
- *Pensavo che avesse mangiato.* (I thought he had eaten: earlier.)

**Watch out:** do not forget the agreement with *essere*: *Credevo che Giulia fosse partita*, not *fosse partito*. And do not use the passato prossimo form after a past main verb: *pensavo che sia partito* is a common slip; say *pensavo che fosse partito*.

Examples:
- *Pensavo che fosse già partito.* (I thought he had already left.)
- *Non sapevo che avessi cambiato casa.* (I didn't know you had moved house.)
- *Era contenta che fossimo venuti.* (She was happy we had come.)

grammarPoints.title: Matching tenses with the subjunctive
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** The tense of the subjunctive depends on two things: the tense of the main verb (the one before *che*), and whether the other action happens at the same time, later, or earlier. Italians call this *concordanza dei tempi*.

| Main verb | Same time or later | Earlier |
|---|---|---|
| present: *penso che* | *venga* | *sia venuto* |
| past: *pensavo che* | *venisse* | *fosse venuto* |
| conditional: *vorrei che* | *venisse* | *fosse venuto* |

So there are two families:
- Main verb in the present (or future, or imperative): use the **present** subjunctive, or the **past** subjunctive (*abbia fatto, sia andato*) for something earlier.
- Main verb in any past tense (imperfetto, passato prossimo) or in the conditional: use the **imperfect** subjunctive, or the **pluperfect** (*avesse fatto, fosse andato*) for something earlier.

Impersonal phrases work the same way: *è importante che venga*, but *era importante che venisse*.

For a future action seen from the past, Italian often uses the past conditional instead: *Ero sicuro che sarebbe venuto.* (I was sure he would come.)

**Watch out:** *vorrei che* talks about now, but it is a conditional, so it takes the imperfect subjunctive: *Vorrei che tu venissi*, never *vorrei che tu venga*. The same goes for *preferirei che*, *sarebbe meglio che*.

Examples:
- *Spero che tu stia bene.* (I hope you're well.)
- *Speravo che tu stessi bene.* (I was hoping you were well.)
- *Non credo che abbiano capito.* (I don't think they understood.)
- *Non credevo che avessero capito.* (I didn't think they had understood.)

grammarPoints.title: Unlikely conditions: se avessi tempo, viaggerei
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** To talk about something imaginary or unlikely, now or in the future ("if I had time, I would travel"), Italian uses **se + imperfect subjunctive** for the condition and the **conditional** for the result.

The pattern:
- *se* + imperfect subjunctive: *se avessi, se fossi, se potessi*
- result in the present conditional: *viaggerei, sarei, potrei*

The two halves can come in either order:
- *Se avessi tempo, viaggerei.*
- *Viaggerei, se avessi tempo.*

Compare the three degrees:
- Real, likely: *Se ho tempo, vengo.* (If I have time, I'll come.) Both verbs in the indicative.
- Unlikely or imaginary: *Se avessi tempo, verrei.* (If I had time, I would come.)
- Impossible, about the past: see the next point.

Useful chunks: *se fossi in te* (if I were you), *se potessi* (if I could), *sarebbe meglio se* (it would be better if).

**Watch out:** never put the conditional after *se*. *Se avrei tempo* is the most famous mistake in Italian, even among natives; say *se avessi tempo*. And English "if I were" or "if I was" is always *se fossi*.

Examples:
- *Se avessi più soldi, comprerei una casa al mare.* (If I had more money, I'd buy a house by the sea.)
- *Se fossi in te, accetterei.* (If I were you, I'd accept.)
- *Cosa faresti se vincessi alla lotteria?* (What would you do if you won the lottery?)

grammarPoints.title: Past unreal conditions: se avessi saputo, sarei venuto
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** To imagine a different past ("if I had known, I would have come"), use **se + pluperfect subjunctive** for the condition and the **past conditional** for the result. The past cannot change, so both halves are unreal.

The pattern:
- *se* + pluperfect subjunctive: *se avessi saputo, se fossi partito*
- result in the past conditional: *sarei venuto, avrei detto*

Both halves choose *avere* or *essere* as in the passato prossimo, and with *essere* the participle agrees with the subject:
- *Se Laura fosse partita prima, sarebbe arrivata in tempo.* (If Laura had left earlier, she would have arrived in time.)

As before, the order can be swapped: *Sarei venuto, se avessi saputo.*

In relaxed speech you will often hear the imperfetto in both halves: *Se lo sapevo, venivo.* It is fine in conversation, but write the full form.

**Watch out:** English "would have" goes only in the result, never after *se*. *Se avrei saputo* and *se sarei venuto* are wrong; the *se* half always takes the subjunctive: *se avessi saputo*. Also check *essere* verbs: *se fossi arrivato*, not *se avessi arrivato*.

Examples:
- *Se avessi saputo, sarei venuto.* (If I had known, I would have come.)
- *Se non avesse piovuto, saremmo andati al mare.* (If it hadn't rained, we would have gone to the seaside.)
- *Se mi avessi chiamato, ti avrei aiutato.* (If you had called me, I would have helped you.)

grammarPoints.title: Subjunctive after benché, affinché, prima che, senza che
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Some conjunctions (linking words that join two parts of a sentence) are always followed by the subjunctive. Learn them as a set.

| Conjunction | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *benché, sebbene, nonostante* | although |
| *affinché, perché* | so that |
| *prima che* | before |
| *senza che* | without |
| *purché, a condizione che* | provided that |
| *a meno che (non)* | unless |

The tense follows the usual rule: present or past subjunctive after a present main verb, imperfect or pluperfect after a past one.
- *Esco, benché piova.* (I'm going out, although it's raining.)
- *È uscito senza che nessuno lo vedesse.* (He went out without anyone seeing him.)

*Perché* with the subjunctive means "so that"; with the indicative it means "because": *Parlo piano perché dorme* (because he's sleeping) versus *Parlo piano perché non si svegli* (so that he doesn't wake up).

After *a meno che* Italians usually add a *non* that does not make the sentence negative: *a meno che non piova* (unless it rains).

**Watch out:** *prima che*, *senza che* and *affinché* are for two different subjects. When the subject is the same, use a preposition + infinitive (the *-are, -ere, -ire* form): *prima di partire*, *senza dire niente*, *per capire*. So "before I leave, I'll call you" is *prima di partire ti chiamo*, not *prima che io parta*.

Examples:
- *Benché fosse stanca, ha continuato a lavorare.* (Although she was tired, she kept working.)
- *Te lo spiego affinché tu capisca.* (I'm explaining it to you so that you understand.)
- *Ti presto la macchina, purché tu guidi con attenzione.* (I'll lend you the car, provided you drive carefully.)

grammarPoints.title: Subjunctive in relative clauses: cerco qualcuno che sappia
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** A relative clause (a part of the sentence starting with *che*, "who, which, that", describing a noun) takes the subjunctive when that person or thing is wanted, imagined or may not exist. When it really exists, use the indicative.

Compare:
- *Conosco una ragazza che parla cinese.* (I know a girl who speaks Chinese: she exists.)
- *Cerco una ragazza che parli cinese.* (I'm looking for a girl who speaks Chinese: any girl, if there is one.)

The subjunctive is used:
- after looking for, wanting, needing: *cerco, vorrei, ho bisogno di* + someone or something *che*...
- after a negative: *non c'è nessuno che*, *non ho trovato niente che*
- after a superlative or *l'unico, il primo, l'ultimo*: *il film più bello che abbia visto*, *l'unica persona che mi capisca*
- often in questions about whether something exists: *C'è qualcuno che sappia la strada?*

The tense follows the main verb as usual: *cerco qualcuno che sappia*, but *cercavo qualcuno che sapesse*.

**Watch out:** English uses the same verb form in both cases, so learners forget the switch. Ask yourself: do I have a real, specific person or thing in mind? If yes, indicative (*ho un collega che vive a Bologna*); if not, subjunctive (*cerco un collega che viva a Bologna*).

Examples:
- *Cerco qualcuno che sappia il tedesco.* (I'm looking for someone who knows German.)
- *Non c'è niente che io possa fare.* (There's nothing I can do.)
- *È il libro più bello che abbia mai letto.* (It's the best book I've ever read.)

grammarPoints.title: As if: come se + imperfect subjunctive
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** *Come se* means "as if" or "as though". It is always followed by the imperfect or the pluperfect subjunctive, whatever the tense of the main verb.

Which one to use:
- **imperfect subjunctive** for something at the same time: *Parla come se fosse il capo.* (He talks as if he were the boss.)
- **pluperfect subjunctive** for something earlier: *Mangia come se non avesse mangiato da giorni.* (He eats as if he hadn't eaten for days.)

The main verb can be present, past or future; it does not change the choice:
- *Mi guarda come se non mi conoscesse.* (She looks at me as if she didn't know me.)
- *Mi guardava come se non mi conoscesse.* (She looked at me as if she didn't know me.)

A common set phrase: *Fai come se fossi a casa tua.* (Make yourself at home.) Another: *come se niente fosse* (as if nothing had happened, casually).

**Watch out:** English often says "as if he was" or "like he's the boss". Italian never uses the indicative or the present subjunctive here: not *come se è*, not *come se sia*, but *come se fosse*.

Examples:
- *Parla come se sapesse tutto.* (He talks as if he knew everything.)
- *Si comportavano come se niente fosse successo.* (They behaved as if nothing had happened.)
- *Mi sento come se avessi corso una maratona.* (I feel as if I had run a marathon.)

grammarPoints.title: Passive with venire and andare: viene servito, va fatto
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Besides *essere*, Italian can make the passive with **venire** (to stress the action) and with **andare** (meaning "must be done").

**Venire + past participle** means the same as the *essere* passive, but it clearly describes an action, not a state:
- *La porta è chiusa.* (The door is closed: a state, or is being closed?)
- *La porta viene chiusa alle otto.* (The door is closed at eight: someone closes it.)

It is used only in simple (one-word) tenses of *venire*: *viene, veniva, verrà, verrebbe, venga*. In compound tenses use *essere*: *è stato servito*, never *è venuto servito*.

**Andare + past participle** means something must or should be done:
- *Questo lavoro va fatto entro domani.* (This work must be done by tomorrow.)
- *I documenti vanno firmati.* (The documents must be signed.)
- *Non va detto a nessuno.* (It mustn't be told to anyone.)

The participle agrees with the subject in both cases: *la cena viene servita*, *le verdure vanno lavate*.

With verbs of losing and destroying, *andare* simply means "get": *andare perso* (to get lost), *andare distrutto* (to be destroyed). Here compound tenses are fine: *molti libri sono andati persi*.

**Watch out:** *va fatto* has nothing to do with going. Read it as "needs to be done". And keep *venire* out of compound tenses.

Examples:
- *La cena viene servita alle otto.* (Dinner is served at eight.)
- *Questa medicina va presa dopo i pasti.* (This medicine must be taken after meals.)
- *Il pane veniva fatto in casa ogni mattina.* (Bread used to be made at home every morning.)

grammarPoints.title: Passive si: si vendono biglietti
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** *Si* + a verb in the third person is the most common Italian passive in everyday speech: *si vendono biglietti* (tickets are sold). The verb agrees with the thing: singular for one thing, plural for several.

How it works:
- one thing: *si vende* una casa, *si parla* italiano
- several things: *si vendono* biglietti, *si parlano* quattro lingue

English often translates it with "you", "people" or "they": *Come si scrive?* (How do you spell it?) *A Natale si mangia il panettone.* (At Christmas people eat panettone.)

In compound tenses (two-word tenses) it always uses *essere*, and the participle agrees with the thing:
- *Si è venduta una sola casa.* (Only one house was sold.)
- *Si sono venduti molti biglietti.* (A lot of tickets were sold.)
- *Si sono trovate nuove soluzioni.* (New solutions were found.)

It works in every tense: *si scrivevano* (used to be written), *si decideranno* (will be decided).

Compare with the impersonal *si* you already know, which has no thing after it and stays singular: *Qui si vive bene.* (People live well here.)

**Watch out:** the verb must agree with the noun. *Si vende biglietti* and *si parla quattro lingue* are common slips, even in Italian shop signs; the correct forms are *si vendono biglietti* and *si parlano quattro lingue*.

Examples:
- *Qui si vendono biglietti dell'autobus.* (Bus tickets are sold here.)
- *In Svizzera si parlano quattro lingue.* (Four languages are spoken in Switzerland.)
- *Non si è trovata una soluzione.* (No solution was found.)

grammarPoints.title: Passato remoto: the narrative past
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** The *passato remoto* is a one-word past tense for completed events. It is the tense of history books, novels and fairy tales. In everyday speech most Italians use the passato prossimo instead, though it is still common in speech in the south and in Tuscany.

Regular forms:

| | parlare | dormire |
|---|---|---|
| io | parlai | dormii |
| tu | parlasti | dormisti |
| lui, lei | parlò | dormì |
| noi | parlammo | dormimmo |
| voi | parlaste | dormiste |
| loro | parlarono | dormirono |

Regular *-ere* verbs have two sets of forms (*credei* or *credetti*); most common *-ere* verbs are irregular anyway.

Irregular verbs usually change only in three persons, io, lui/lei and loro, and are regular in the others:
- *fare*: feci, facesti, fece, facemmo, faceste, fecero
- *avere*: ebbi, avesti, ebbe, avemmo, aveste, ebbero
- *essere* (fully irregular): fui, fosti, fu, fummo, foste, furono

More io forms to learn: *dissi* (dire), *venni* (venire), *vidi* (vedere), *presi* (prendere), *scrissi* (scrivere), *nacqui* (nascere), *vissi* (vivere), *decisi* (decidere), *dipinsi* (dipingere), *diedi* (dare), *stetti* (stare).

It is used like the passato prossimo, next to the imperfetto for background: *Quando arrivò, pioveva.* (When he arrived, it was raining.)

**Watch out:** the accent matters: *parlò* (he spoke) is not *parlo* (I speak), and *finì* (he finished) is not *fini*. For reading, learn the lui and loro forms first; they are the ones you meet most.

Examples:
- *Dante nacque a Firenze nel 1265.* (Dante was born in Florence in 1265.)
- *La guerra finì nel 1945.* (The war ended in 1945.)
- *Disse che era stanco e se ne andò.* (He said he was tired and left.)

grammarPoints.title: Reported speech: ha detto che sarebbe venuto
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Reported speech (*discorso indiretto*) tells what someone said without quoting them: "Marco said he was tired". When the reporting verb (*ha detto, disse, diceva*) is in the past, the verbs inside move one step back in time.

| They said | Reported after *ha detto che* |
|---|---|
| *Sono stanco.* | *era stanco* |
| *Ho finito.* | *aveva finito* |
| *Verrò.* | *sarebbe venuto* |
| *Vieni!* | *di venire* |

So:
- present becomes imperfetto
- passato prossimo becomes trapassato prossimo (*aveva finito*)
- future becomes past conditional (*sarebbe venuto*)
- present subjunctive becomes imperfect subjunctive
- an order (imperative) becomes *di* + infinitive: *mi ha detto di tornare presto*. *Che* + imperfect subjunctive (*mi ha detto che tornassi presto*) also exists, but it is formal and old-fashioned
- a yes or no question uses *se* (if): *mi ha chiesto se volevo un caffè*

Pronouns, possessives and time words change too: *io* becomes *lui* or *lei*, *qui* becomes *lì*, *oggi* becomes *quel giorno*, *domani* becomes *il giorno dopo*, *ieri* becomes *il giorno prima*.

If the reporting verb is in the present (*dice che*), nothing moves: *Dice che è stanco.*

**Watch out:** English "he said he would come" uses "would", but Italian needs the **past** conditional here: *ha detto che sarebbe venuto*. *Ha detto che verrebbe* sounds wrong to a careful speaker.

Examples:
- *Luca ha detto che sarebbe venuto alla festa.* (Luca said he would come to the party.)
- *Giulia mi ha detto che aveva finito il progetto.* (Giulia told me she had finished the project.)
- *La professoressa ci ha detto di studiare di più.* (The teacher told us to study more.)

grammarPoints.title: Il quale, chi, quello che, ciò che
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Besides *che* and *cui*, Italian has *il quale* (a more formal "who, which"), *chi* ("whoever, the person who") and *quello che* or *ciò che* ("what, the thing that").

**Il quale** agrees with the noun it refers to: *il quale, la quale, i quali, le quali*. It can replace *che* or *cui*, and it combines with prepositions and their articles: *con la quale, del quale, per i quali, alla quale*.
- *Ecco la collega con la quale lavoro.* (= *con cui lavoro*)
It is more formal, and useful when *che* would be unclear, because it shows gender and number: *la sorella di Marco, la quale vive a Parigi* (the sister lives in Paris, not Marco).

**Chi** means "the person who" or "whoever". It takes a singular verb and is common in proverbs and rules:
- *Chi cerca trova.* (Seek and you shall find.)
- *C'è chi preferisce il mare.* (Some people prefer the sea.)

**Quello che** and **ciò che** mean "what" in the sense "the thing that". They are interchangeable; *ciò che* is a little more written. *Tutto quello che* or *tutto ciò che* means "everything that".
- *Non ho capito quello che hai detto.* (I didn't understand what you said.)

**Watch out:** English "what" in the middle of a sentence is not *che* or *cosa* here: "What I need is rest" is *Quello che mi serve è riposo*. And "those who" with *chi* stays singular: *chi arriva tardi*, not *chi arrivano tardi*.

Examples:
- *Ti dirò tutto quello che so.* (I'll tell you everything I know.)
- *Chi arriva tardi non trova posto.* (Whoever arrives late won't find a seat.)
- *Sono i motivi per i quali ho rinunciato.* (These are the reasons why I gave up.)

grammarPoints.title: Pronominal verbs: andarsene, farcela, cavarsela
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Some very common verbs come with one or two pronouns glued on, and this changes their meaning: *andarsene* (to leave), *farcela* (to manage), *cavarsela* (to get by). You learn them as fixed expressions.

**Andarsene** (to go away, leave): *me ne vado, te ne vai, se ne va, ce ne andiamo, ve ne andate, se ne vanno*. Passato prossimo with *essere*: *me ne sono andato/a*. Imperative: *vattene!* (go away!), *andiamocene* (let's go).

**Farcela** (to manage, to make it, to cope): *ce la faccio, ce la fai, ce la fa, ce la facciamo, ce la fate, ce la fanno*. Passato prossimo: *ce l'ho fatta* (I made it).

**Cavarsela** (to get by, to cope all right): *me la cavo, te la cavi, se la cava, ce la caviamo, ve la cavate, se la cavano*. Passato prossimo: *me la sono cavata*.

A few more:
- *prendersela* (to get upset, take offence): *Non te la prendere!* *Se l'è presa.*
- *avercela con qualcuno* (to be angry with someone): *Ce l'hai con me?*
- *fregarsene* (not to care, informal): *Me ne frego.*

Notice the spelling: *mi, ti, si, ci, vi* become *me, te, se, ce, ve* before *ne* and *la*.

**Watch out:** in compound tenses the participle of the *-la* verbs is always feminine, because it agrees with *la*: *ce l'abbiamo fatta*, *Marco se l'è cavata*, never *fatto* or *cavato*. With *andarsene* it agrees with the subject: *Giulia se n'è andata*.

Examples:
- *È tardi, me ne vado.* (It's late, I'm off.)
- *Non ce la faccio più!* (I can't take any more!)
- *Con l'inglese me la cavo.* (I get by in English.)

grammarPoints.title: Fare + infinitive: faccio riparare la macchina
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** *Fare* + an infinitive (the dictionary form of a verb) means "to have something done" or "to make someone do something": *Faccio riparare la macchina.* (I'm having the car repaired.) *Mi fa ridere.* (He makes me laugh.)

How it works:
- *fare* changes for person and tense; the infinitive never changes: *faccio riparare, ho fatto riparare, farò riparare*.
- the person made to act is a direct object (*lo, la, li, le*) if there is no other object: *La faccio ridere.* (I make her laugh.)
- if there is also a thing, the person takes *a* and becomes indirect (*gli, le*): *Faccio leggere il libro a Marco.* becomes *Glielo faccio leggere.*

For something done for yourself, use **farsi** + infinitive, with *essere* in compound tenses: *Mi faccio tagliare i capelli.* (I'm getting my hair cut.) *Mi sono fatta tagliare i capelli.* (I had my hair cut, said by a woman.)

Pronouns go before *fare*, or attach to it in the imperative and infinitive: *fallo entrare* (let him in), *voglio farti vedere una cosa*. Before another infinitive, *fare* is often shortened to *far*: *far vedere* (to show).

In the passato prossimo, the participle agrees with a *lo, la, li, le* before it: *La lavatrice? L'ho fatta riparare.*

**Watch out:** the pronouns belong to *fare*, not to the second verb: *la faccio riparare*, never *faccio ripararla*. And English "get" or "have" something done is not *avere*: say *ho fatto riparare*, not *ho avuto riparato*.

Examples:
- *Il film mi ha fatto piangere.* (The film made me cry.)
- *Dove hai fatto stampare le foto?* (Where did you get the photos printed?)
- *Non farmi aspettare!* (Don't keep me waiting!)

grammarPoints.title: Highlighting: il libro l'ho letto, è lui che...
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Spoken Italian often moves a word to the front to make it the topic, then repeats it with a pronoun: *Il libro l'ho letto.* (The book, I've read it.) To stress who or what, it uses *è ... che*: *È Marco che ha chiamato.* (It was Marco who called.)

**Moving the object to the front.** When the direct object (the "what?" of the verb) comes first, you must repeat it with *lo, la, li, le* before the verb:
- *Il caffè lo prendo senza zucchero.*
- *La pasta la compro io.*
- *Le chiavi le ho perse.* (the participle agrees, as usual with *lo, la, li, le*)

The same happens with *ne* for amounts and *di* phrases (*Di soldi non ne ho*), with *ci* for places (*A Roma ci sono stato*), and with indirect objects (*A Luca gli ho scritto* is very common in speech; *A Luca ho scritto* is safer in writing).

The topic can also come at the end, as an afterthought: *L'hai vista, la nuova casa?*

**Stressing one element (cleft sentences).** Use *è* + the stressed part + *che*:
- *È Marco che ha telefonato, non Luca.*
- *È per questo che non sono venuto.* (That's why I didn't come.)
For the subject, *è stato ... a* + infinitive is very natural: *È stata mia sorella a dirmelo.* (It was my sister who told me.)

**Watch out:** English can say "The book I've read" with no pronoun, but in Italian an object moved to the front needs its pronoun: *Il libro l'ho letto*, not *Il libro ho letto* (that sounds like a strong contrast, or simply odd).

Examples:
- *Quel film l'ho visto due volte.* (I've seen that film twice.)
- *I compiti li fai dopo.* (You'll do your homework later.)
- *È lui che mi ha aiutato.* (He's the one who helped me.)

grammarPoints.title: Suffixes: -ino, -etto, -one, -accio
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Italian adds endings to nouns to make them small, big or bad, often with feeling: *gatto* (cat) becomes *gattino* (kitten), *libro* becomes *librone* (big book), *tempo* becomes *tempaccio* (awful weather).

Drop the final vowel and add the suffix (the added ending). It still agrees in gender and number.

| Suffix | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *-ino, -ina* | small, cute | *gattino, manina* |
| *-etto, -etta* | small | *casetta, laghetto* |
| *-one, -ona* | big | *librone, nasone* |
| *-accio, -accia* | bad, ugly | *tempaccio, parolaccia* |

Some notes:
- After *c* and *g*, add *h* to keep the hard sound: *lago* gives *laghetto*, *barca* gives *barchetta*.
- For family, *-ino* often means younger: *fratellino* (little brother), *sorellina*.
- *-accio* can be playful for people: *ragazzaccio* (naughty boy).
- *-one* often turns a feminine noun masculine: *la porta* gives *il portone* (main door of a building).

Many altered words have become ordinary words with their own meaning: *panino* (sandwich, from *pane*), *ombrellone* (beach umbrella), *portone* (front door), *telefonino* (mobile phone), *parolaccia* (swear word).

**Watch out:** you cannot add any suffix to any word. Some forms do not exist, and some mean something else: *burrone* is a ravine, not a lot of butter, and *mulino* is a mill, not a small mule. Use the ones you have heard, and learn the fixed words as new vocabulary.

Examples:
- *Abbiamo trovato un gattino sotto la macchina.* (We found a kitten under the car.)
- *Che tempaccio oggi!* (What awful weather today!)
- *Ho un fratellino di sei anni.* (I've got a little brother who's six.)

grammarPoints.title: Participle clauses: finita la cena, ...
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** a past participle on its own at the start of a sentence means "once this was done" or "after doing this". It is a compact, written-style alternative to *dopo che* or *dopo aver*.

*Finita la cena, siamo usciti.* = *Dopo che la cena è finita, siamo usciti.*

How it agrees (agreement means the ending matches in gender and number):
- With a verb that takes an object (the thing acted on), the participle agrees with that object, which usually comes right after it: *finita la cena*, *chiuse le finestre*, *letto il giornale*.
- With a verb that takes *essere* (arrive, leave, go out...), it agrees with the subject (who does the action): *Arrivati a casa, ci siamo riposati.* *Partita Giulia, ...*
- Object pronouns and reflexive pronouns are attached to the end: *vistolo* (having seen him), *alzatasi* (she having got up).

You often add *una volta* for "once": *Una volta presa la decisione, ...*

The participle clause usually describes something that happened before the main action. It sounds natural in writing, news and storytelling; in everyday speech *dopo che* or *quando* is more common.

**Watch out:** do not add *avendo* or *essendo* here, and do not leave the ending as *-o* by default. *Finito la cena* is wrong: it must be *finita*, because *cena* is feminine.

Examples:
- *Finita la cena, siamo usciti a fare due passi.* (Once dinner was over, we went out for a walk.)
- *Arrivate a Roma, le ragazze hanno chiamato i genitori.* (Once they reached Rome, the girls called their parents.)
- *Una volta firmato il contratto, non si può più cambiare idea.* (Once the contract is signed, you can't change your mind.)
- *Vistolo arrivare, la madre gli corse incontro.* (Seeing him arrive, his mother ran to meet him.)

grammarPoints.title: Past gerund: avendo finito, essendo arrivati
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the past gerund means "having done something". Use it for an action that happened before the main action, often as its cause: *Avendo finito, sono uscito.* (Having finished, I went out.)

It is built with the gerund of the auxiliary (the helping verb *avere* or *essere*) plus the past participle:

| auxiliary | example |
|---|---|
| *avendo* | *avendo finito, avendo letto* |
| *essendo* | *essendo arrivato, essendo partite* |

- Choose *avendo* or *essendo* exactly as in the passato prossimo: *ho finito*, so *avendo finito*; *sono arrivato*, so *essendo arrivato*.
- With *essendo*, the participle agrees with the subject: *essendo arrivata* (Sara), *essendo arrivati* (we).
- Pronouns attach to the end of *avendo* or *essendo*: *avendolo visto* (having seen it), *essendosi alzata* (she having got up), *avendoci pensato* (having thought about it).
- For the negative, put *non* first: *non avendo capito* (not having understood).

The subject of the gerund should be the same as the subject of the main verb: *Avendo perso il treno, abbiamo preso un taxi* (we lost it, we took the taxi).

**Watch out:** English "having" tempts you to always use *avendo*. Verbs that take *essere* need *essendo*: *essendo partito*, not *avendo partito*. And with *essendo*, remember the agreement.

Examples:
- *Avendo studiato molto, Sara ha superato l'esame.* (Having studied a lot, Sara passed the exam.)
- *Essendo arrivati tardi, abbiamo perso l'inizio del film.* (Having arrived late, we missed the start of the film.)
- *Non avendo ricevuto risposta, ho scritto di nuovo.* (Not having had a reply, I wrote again.)
- *Essendosi rotta una gamba, Chiara non può sciare.* (Having broken her leg, Chiara can't ski.)

grammarPoints.title: Mixed and implicit if-clauses
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the "if" part and the result part of an unreal sentence can refer to different times, so you mix the two patterns you know. And the condition can also be hidden in a gerund, *a* + infinitive or a phrase like *senza di te*.

Mixed patterns:

| if part | result | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *se avessi studiato* | *ora avrei un lavoro* | past cause, present result |
| *se fossi più paziente* | *non avrei litigato* | general fact, past result |

- Past condition, present result: *se* + pluperfect subjunctive (*avessi fatto*) + present conditional (*farei*).
- Present or permanent condition, past result: *se* + imperfect subjunctive (*fossi*) + past conditional (*avrei fatto*).

Implicit conditions (no *se*):
- gerund: *Volendo, potremmo partire domani.* (If we wanted to...)
- *a* + infinitive: *A saperlo, sarei venuto.* (Had I known...)
- a phrase: *senza il tuo aiuto*, *al tuo posto*, *con un po' di fortuna*.

In relaxed speech, the past unreal sentence is often said with two imperfects: *Se lo sapevo, venivo.* (= *Se l'avessi saputo, sarei venuto.*) It is very common but stay with the subjunctive in writing.

**Watch out:** never use the conditional in the *se* part (the condition) of an if-sentence. *Se avrei studiato* is a classic mistake (also for Italians): it must be *se avessi studiato*.

Examples:
- *Se avessi studiato medicina, ora farei il medico.* (If I had studied medicine, I'd be a doctor now.)
- *Se non fossi così testardo, avresti accettato il loro aiuto.* (If you weren't so stubborn, you'd have accepted their help.)
- *Senza il tuo aiuto, non ce l'avrei fatta.* (Without your help, I wouldn't have made it.)
- *A saperlo, sarei venuto prima.* (Had I known, I'd have come earlier.)

grammarPoints.title: Conditional for unconfirmed news: sarebbe stato arrestato
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** news reports use the conditional to give information that is not confirmed: the reporter is passing it on, not vouching for it. In English you say "reportedly", "allegedly" or "is said to".

- For something true now, use the **present conditional**: *Il ministro sarebbe pronto a dimettersi.* (The minister is reportedly ready to resign.)
- For something that happened, use the **past conditional** (the conditional of *avere* or *essere* + past participle): *Il ladro sarebbe entrato dalla finestra.* (The thief allegedly got in through the window.)
- For a passive (something done to the subject), use *sarebbe stato* + participle: *Il sospettato sarebbe stato arrestato.* (The suspect has reportedly been arrested.)
- For something in progress: *starebbe lavorando* (is reportedly working).

This conditional often comes with *secondo* (according to), *stando a* (going by), *a quanto pare* (apparently). (After *pare che* you need the subjunctive instead: *pare che sia pronto*.) The same rules for agreement apply as in the passato prossimo: *la coppia si sarebbe separata*.

It is the standard tool of Italian newspapers and TV news, and you also use it in speech when you repeat gossip.

**Watch out:** this conditional has nothing to do with "would". Translate *sarebbe stato arrestato* as "has reportedly been arrested", not "would have been arrested". And do not change it into the indicative: the conditional is exactly what signals "not confirmed".

Examples:
- *Secondo alcune fonti, il ministro sarebbe pronto a dimettersi.* (According to some sources, the minister is ready to resign.)
- *Il sospettato sarebbe stato arrestato ieri sera.* (The suspect was reportedly arrested last night.)
- *Nell'incidente ci sarebbero tre feriti.* (Three people are reported injured in the accident.)
- *Il cantante starebbe lavorando a un nuovo album.* (The singer is said to be working on a new album.)

grammarPoints.title: The subjunctive on its own: Magari!, Che entri!, Sia chiaro
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the subjunctive can stand alone, with no main verb before it, to express a wish, a wondering question, or a "let him / let them" order.

Wishes, with *magari* or *se solo* (if only):
- imperfect subjunctive for now: *Magari fosse vero!* (If only it were true!)
- pluperfect subjunctive for the past: *Magari fossimo partiti prima!* (If only we had left earlier!)

*Che* + subjunctive (present, or past for something already done):
- an order or permission about someone else (third person): *Che entri pure.* (Let him come in.) *Che se ne vadano!* (Let them go!)
- a wondering question: *Che sia già partito?* (Could he have left already?) *Che abbia dimenticato?* (Could she have forgotten?)

Fixed expressions you will meet often:
- *Sia chiaro.* (Let's be clear.)
- *Che io sappia...* (As far as I know...)
- *Viva gli sposi!* (Long live the bride and groom!) *Viva* usually stays singular even before a plural; *Vivano* is correct but formal.
- *Dio ce ne scampi!* (God forbid!)

These forms sound natural in speech and writing alike; *magari* and *che io sappia* are everyday Italian.

**Watch out:** after *magari* meaning "if only", use the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive, never the present or the conditional: *Magari potessi!*, not *Magari posso!* or *Magari potrei!* (On its own, *magari* also means "maybe", and then it takes the indicative: *Magari vengo.*)

Examples:
- *Magari avessi più tempo!* (If only I had more time!)
- *Il signor Bianchi è qui? Che entri pure.* (Mr Bianchi's here? Let him come in.)
- *Non risponde: che sia già partito?* (He isn't answering: could he have left already?)
- *Che io sappia, il negozio è aperto.* (As far as I know, the shop is open.)

grammarPoints.title: Subjunctive after superlatives and in indirect questions
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** careful Italian uses the subjunctive in two more places: after a superlative or *l'unico* (the only one) followed by *che*, and in indirect questions (a question reported inside a sentence: "I wonder where he is").

After superlatives, *il primo*, *l'ultimo*, *l'unico*:
- *È il film più bello che io abbia mai visto.* (It's the best film I've ever seen.)
- *Sei l'unica persona che mi capisca.* (You're the only person who understands me.)

Indirect questions, after *non so*, *mi chiedo*, *mi domando*, *non capisco*, *chiedere* + *se, chi, dove, come, perché, quanto*:
- *Non so se sia vero.* (I don't know if it's true.)
- *Mi chiedo dove abbiano messo le chiavi.* (I wonder where they've put the keys.)

The sequence of tenses applies as usual. With a main verb in the past, use the imperfect subjunctive for the same time and the pluperfect for earlier:
- *Mi domandavo chi fosse.* (I wondered who she was.)
- *Non sapevamo se il volo fosse partito.* (We didn't know if the flight had left.)

In everyday speech the indicative is also common here (*Non so se è vero*), but in writing and formal speech the subjunctive is expected.

**Watch out:** in the present subjunctive the *io*, *tu* and *lui/lei* forms are the same (*che io abbia, che tu abbia, che lui abbia*), so keep the subject pronoun when it is not clear: *il film più bello che io abbia visto*. In an indirect question, *se* means "whether".

Examples:
- *È la persona più generosa che io conosca.* (She's the most generous person I know.)
- *Non capisco perché tu non voglia venire.* (I don't understand why you don't want to come.)
- *Gli ho chiesto quanto costasse la riparazione.* (I asked him how much the repair cost.)

grammarPoints.title: Whose: il cui, la cui
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** "whose" in Italian is article + *cui* + noun: *l'uomo la cui moglie...* (the man whose wife...). The article agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner.

| possessed noun | whose |
|---|---|
| masculine singular | *il cui padre* |
| feminine singular | *la cui casa* |
| masculine plural | *i cui libri* |
| feminine plural | *le cui strade* |

- *Ho conosciuto un uomo la cui moglie è giapponese.* (*la* because *moglie* is feminine, even though the owner is a man.)
- *È una scrittrice i cui libri sono famosi.* (*i* because *libri* is masculine plural.)

With a preposition (a small linking word like *in, a, di*), join it to the article as usual (*in + la = nella*) and put it before *cui*:
- *la signora nella cui casa abitavo* (the lady in whose house I lived)
- *un problema alla cui soluzione lavoriamo* (a problem whose solution we're working on)
- *un'attrice del cui passato si sa poco* (an actress about whose past little is known)

*Il cui* belongs to written and careful spoken Italian. In conversation people often rephrase: *un uomo che ha la moglie giapponese*. A more formal alternative is *del quale / della quale* after the noun: *l'uomo, la moglie del quale...*

**Watch out:** do not match the article to the owner. *La donna il cui marito* is right (*marito* is masculine); *la donna la cui marito* is wrong. And never put *di* before *cui* for "whose": *l'uomo di cui la moglie* is wrong.

Examples:
- *Il ragazzo il cui padre lavora con me si chiama Luca.* (The boy whose father works with me is called Luca.)
- *Ho visitato una città le cui strade erano piene di turisti.* (I visited a city whose streets were full of tourists.)
- *La signora nella cui casa abitavo era molto gentile.* (The lady in whose house I lived was very kind.)

grammarPoints.title: Lasciare, sentire, vedere + infinitive; farsi fare
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** like *fare*, the verbs *lasciare* (let), *vedere* (see), *sentire* (hear) and *guardare* (watch) can be followed directly by an infinitive (the basic *-are/-ere/-ire* form). *Farsi* + infinitive means "to get something done for yourself".

*lasciare* + infinitive:
- *I miei non mi lasciano uscire.* (My parents don't let me go out.)
- *Lascialo parlare!* (Let him speak!)
- *Non lasciarti convincere.* (Don't let yourself be talked into it.)
- *lasciare che* + subjunctive is the alternative: *Ha lasciato che tutti partissero.*

*vedere, sentire, guardare* + infinitive, with no preposition before the infinitive:
- *Ho sentito Marta cantare.* (I heard Marta sing.)
- *Ho visto i bambini correre.* (I saw the children running.)
