- An object pronoun goes before the conjugated verb, and in the passato prossimo the participle agrees with it: *Li ho visti correre.*

*farsi* + infinitive (have something done for yourself, or get someone to do something for you). It takes *essere*, so the participle agrees with the subject:
- *Mi sono fatto tagliare i capelli.* (I got my hair cut: a man speaking.)
- *Laura si è fatta aiutare da un amico.* (Laura got a friend to help her.)
- Imperative: *Fatti spiegare la strada.* (Get someone to explain the way to you.)

**Watch out:** English says "I saw them running"; Italian uses the plain infinitive, not the gerund: *Li ho visti correre*, not *Li ho visti correndo*. And with *farsi*, do not use *avere*: *mi sono fatto*, not *mi ho fatto*.

Examples:
- *Lascia stare, ci penso io.* (Leave it, I'll take care of it.)
- *Abbiamo sentito qualcuno bussare alla porta.* (We heard someone knock at the door.)
- *Mi sono fatta portare una pizza.* (I had a pizza delivered: a woman speaking.)

grammarPoints.title: Trapassato remoto: dopo che ebbe finito
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** the trapassato remoto ("had done") is a literary tense. You only need to recognise and use it in one situation: after *dopo che*, *appena*, *non appena* or *quando*, when the main verb is in the passato remoto (the simple past of written stories).

It is the passato remoto of *avere* or *essere* + the past participle:

| | avere | essere |
|---|---|---|
| io | *ebbi finito* | *fui partito/a* |
| tu | *avesti finito* | *fosti partito/a* |
| lui, lei | *ebbe finito* | *fu partito/a* |
| noi | *avemmo finito* | *fummo partiti/e* |
| voi | *aveste finito* | *foste partiti/e* |
| loro | *ebbero finito* | *furono partiti/e* |

- Choose the auxiliary (the helping verb) as in the passato prossimo; with *essere*, the participle agrees with the subject.
- Reflexive verbs use *essere*: *si fu seduto* (he had sat down).

*Dopo che ebbe finito di mangiare, uscì.* (After he had finished eating, he went out.) The trapassato remoto shows the action finished just before the main one.

In modern speech and most writing it is replaced by the trapassato prossimo (*dopo che aveva finito*), by *dopo aver finito*, or by a participle clause (*finito di mangiare*). You will meet it in novels and history books.

**Watch out:** do not use it as a general "had done". In any other context, or with a main verb that is not in the passato remoto, use the trapassato prossimo: *Quando sono arrivato, Marco era già uscito.*

Examples:
- *Dopo che ebbe finito di mangiare, il vecchio uscì in giardino.* (After he had finished eating, the old man went out into the garden.)
- *Appena fu arrivata a casa, Maria telefonò alla madre.* (As soon as she had got home, Maria phoned her mother.)
- *Quando ebbero letto la lettera, scoppiarono a ridere.* (When they had read the letter, they burst out laughing.)

grammarPoints.title: Formal conditions and concessions: qualora, purché, per quanto
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** these conjunctions (linking words that join two parts of a sentence) introduce a condition ("if", "provided that", "unless") or a concession ("however much", "although"). All of them are followed by the subjunctive.

Conditions:
- *qualora* (if, in the event that; formal): *Qualora il volo fosse cancellato, vi rimborseremo.*
- *nel caso in cui / nel caso che* (in case): *Nel caso in cui dovesse piovere, ...*
- *purché* (provided that): *Puoi uscire, purché torni presto.*
- *a patto che / a condizione che* (on condition that)
- *ammesso che* (assuming that)
- *a meno che (non)* (unless): *a meno che non venga anche tu*. The *non* here does not make it negative.

Concessions:
- *per quanto* (however much, although): *Per quanto mi sforzi, non ricordo.*
- *nonostante / malgrado* (despite the fact that): *Nonostante fosse stanco, ...*

"-ever" words, also + subjunctive:
- *chiunque* (whoever), *qualunque / qualsiasi* + noun (whatever, whichever), *comunque* (however, whichever way), *dovunque* (wherever).
- *Qualunque cosa tu decida, ti sosterrò.* (Whatever you decide, I'll support you.)

*Qualora* often takes the imperfect subjunctive even for a future event, and *dovesse* + infinitive is common after *qualora* and *nel caso in cui*: *qualora dovesse servire* (should it be needed).

**Watch out:** *a meno che non venga* means "unless he comes", not "unless he doesn't come". And *comunque* + subjunctive means "however / whichever way" (*comunque vada*); on its own with the indicative, it just means "anyway".

Examples:
- *Ti presto la macchina, a patto che tu me la restituisca con il pieno.* (I'll lend you the car on condition that you give it back with a full tank.)
- *Per quanto mi sforzi, non riesco a ricordare il suo nome.* (However hard I try, I can't remember his name.)
- *Comunque vada, sarà un'esperienza utile.* (Whichever way it goes, it'll be a useful experience.)

grammarPoints.title: Formal register: Loro, letters, bureaucratic Italian
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** formal written Italian (letters, emails to offices, notices) has its own fixed phrases, and very formal speech can address a group as *Loro*. You need to recognise all of it and use the common letter formulas yourself.

Letters and formal emails:
- Opening: *Gentile signora Rossi*, *Gentile dottore*, *Egregio avvocato* (very formal, mostly to men). *Gentili signori* for a group.
- *Le scrivo per...* (I am writing to...), *La ringrazio per...* (Thank you for...), *Desidero informarLa che...* (I wish to inform you that...).
- *In allegato Le invio...* (Please find attached...).
- Closing: *In attesa di un Suo cortese riscontro* (Looking forward to your reply), then *Cordiali saluti* or *Distinti saluti*.
- In letters, the formal *Lei* forms are often written with a capital: *La, Le, Suo*, even attached: *informarLa*.

Notices and bureaucratic language:
- *Si prega di* + infinitive (please...): *Si prega di non fumare.*
- *I signori passeggeri sono pregati di...* (Passengers are kindly requested to...)
- *provvedere a* (to see to), *entro* (by a date), *il sottoscritto* (the undersigned).

*Loro* (very formal "you", plural): verbs in the third person plural, *Loro* forms like *Si accomodino* (please sit down), *Desiderano?* (What would you like?). You hear it from waiters in elegant places and in ceremonies; elsewhere *voi* is now normal.

**Watch out:** do not open a formal email with *Caro* + surname or close it with *Ciao*. And *Egregio* is used mostly for men; for a woman *Gentile* is the usual choice (*Egregia* exists but is rarer).

Examples:
- *Gentile dottoressa Rossi, Le scrivo per chiederLe un appuntamento.* (Dear Dr Rossi, I am writing to ask you for an appointment.)
- *Si prega di non lasciare i bagagli incustoditi.* (Please do not leave luggage unattended.)
- *Signori, si accomodino pure.* (Ladies and gentlemen, please take a seat.)

grammarPoints.title: Spoken Italian: mica, pure, magari, allora, cioè, dai
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** discourse markers are the small words that give spoken Italian its tone: they soften, stress, encourage or fill a pause. They rarely translate word for word, but using them makes you sound natural.

- *mica*: strengthens a negative, "not at all", "not exactly". *Non è mica facile.* (It's not exactly easy.) In a question it means "you're not..., are you?": *Non sarai mica arrabbiato?* *Mica male!* (Not bad at all!)
- *pure*: after an imperative, it means "go ahead", "feel free": *Entra pure.* *Fai pure.*
- *magari*: "maybe" (*Magari passo più tardi*), or "I wish!" as an answer: *Hai vinto? Magari!*
- *allora*: "so", "well then", to start or move on: *Allora, che facciamo?*
- *cioè*: "I mean", "that is", to explain or correct: *domani, cioè venerdì*.
- *dai*: "come on", to encourage or to protest: *Dai, non essere triste!* *Su* works the same way.
- *insomma*: "in short", or "so-so" as a lukewarm answer: *Com'è andata? Insomma...*
- *comunque*: "anyway", "still": *Era lungo, ma comunque mi è piaciuto.*
- *figurati*: "don't mention it", "of course not" (*si figuri* with *Lei*).

**Watch out:** *magari* + indicative is "maybe", but *magari!* on its own is "if only!". And *pure* after an imperative is not "also": *Prendi pure* means "go ahead and take it", not "take it too".

Examples:
- *Non è mica facile trovare casa a Milano.* (It's not exactly easy to find a flat in Milan.)
- *Siediti pure, arrivo subito.* (Do sit down, I'll be right there.)
- *Grazie mille! Figurati, è stato un piacere.* (Thanks so much! Don't mention it, it was a pleasure.)
- *Allora, cioè, non so se vengo.* (So, I mean, I don't know if I'm coming.)

grammarPoints.title: Nominalisation: il mangiare, l'arrivo del treno
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** nominalisation means turning a verb or an adjective into a noun (a naming word). Written Italian, especially news and official texts, uses it constantly: *Dopo l'arrivo del treno...* instead of *Dopo che il treno è arrivato...*

Nouns made from verbs. There is no single rule, so learn them in pairs:

| verb | noun |
|---|---|
| *arrivare* | *l'arrivo* |
| *partire* | *la partenza* |
| *aumentare* | *l'aumento* |
| *decidere* | *la decisione* |
| *chiudere* | *la chiusura* |
| *scoprire* | *la scoperta* |

Common endings: *-zione* (*costruzione*), *-mento* (*aumento*, *cambiamento*), *-ura* (*chiusura*), *-enza* (*partenza*), *-ita* (*vendita*, *nascita*). The person or thing involved follows with *di*: *la partenza del volo*, *la nascita del figlio*.

The infinitive as a noun: with *il* (or *lo*, *l'*), an infinitive can act as a masculine noun, often for a habit or way of doing something: *il mangiare*, *il suo continuo lamentarsi* (his constant complaining).

Adjectives as nouns: *il bello* (the nice thing, beauty), *i giovani* (young people), *il difficile* (the hard part).

**Watch out:** English often uses an "-ing" form where Italian needs a real noun: "the closing of the road" is *la chiusura della strada*, not *il chiudere della strada*. Keep the infinitive-noun for general activities and habits.

Examples:
- *Dopo l'arrivo del treno, la stazione si è svuotata.* (After the train arrived, the station emptied.)
- *La chiusura della strada durerà tre giorni.* (The road closure will last three days.)
- *Il bello di questo lavoro è che posso viaggiare.* (The nice thing about this job is that I can travel.)

grammarPoints.title: Essere or avere? Verbs that take both
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** some verbs take *avere* when they have a direct object (a thing acted on directly, with no preposition) and *essere* when they don't. The meaning shifts slightly: someone does something to something, or something simply happens.

| verb | with an object: *avere* | no object: *essere* |
|---|---|---|
| *cominciare* | *Ho cominciato il corso.* | *Il corso è cominciato.* |
| *finire* | *Ho finito il libro.* | *Il film è finito.* |
| *passare* | *Ho passato l'estate qui.* | *Sono passato da te.* |
| *aumentare* | *Hanno aumentato i prezzi.* | *I prezzi sono aumentati.* |

The same pattern works for *iniziare*, *salire*, *scendere* (*ho sceso le scale* / *sono sceso*), *cambiare* (*ho cambiato idea* / *Paolo è cambiato*), *crescere* (*ha cresciuto tre figli* / *è cresciuto*), *diminuire*, *migliorare*.

Other verbs to know:
- *correre*: *avere* for the activity (*Ho corso un'ora*), *essere* with a destination (*Sono corso a casa*).
- Weather verbs take either: *è piovuto* or *ha piovuto*.
- *vivere* takes either without an object: *ho vissuto* or *sono vissuto a Roma*.

With *essere*, the participle agrees with the subject as usual: *la lezione è cominciata*, *i prezzi sono aumentati*.

**Watch out:** ask "is there a direct object?" before choosing. *Ho finito* (I've finished, my work is implied) is right for a person; *è finito* is for the thing that ended. *Il film ha finito* is wrong.

Examples:
- *La lezione è cominciata alle nove.* (The lesson started at nine.)
- *Il professore ha cominciato la lezione in ritardo.* (The teacher started the lesson late.)
- *Mio figlio è cresciuto tantissimo.* (My son has grown so much.)
- *Mia nonna ha cresciuto cinque figli da sola.* (My grandmother raised five children on her own.)

grammarPoints.title: Adjective position changes meaning
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** most adjectives (describing words) go after the noun, with their plain, literal meaning. A few common ones change meaning depending on whether they come before or after the noun.

| adjective | before the noun | after the noun |
|---|---|---|
| *vecchio* | *un vecchio amico* (long-standing) | *un amico vecchio* (elderly) |
| *povero* | *un povero ragazzo* (unlucky) | *un ragazzo povero* (with no money) |
| *grande* | *un grand'uomo* (great) | *un uomo grande* (big) |
| *diverso* | *diversi libri* (several) | *libri diversi* (different) |

More pairs:
- *caro*: *una cara amica* (dear) / *un ristorante caro* (expensive)
- *nuovo*: *una nuova macchina* (another one, new to me) / *una macchina nuova* (brand-new)
- *stesso*: *lo stesso problema* (the same) / *il direttore stesso* (the manager himself)
- *certo*: *un certo coraggio* (a certain amount of) / *una notizia certa* (sure, reliable)
- *unico*: *l'unico figlio* (the only son) / *un figlio unico* (an only child)

The general idea: after the noun, the adjective sorts and describes objectively (which one? a cheap or an expensive one?). Before the noun, it is more subjective, emotional or figurative.

**Watch out:** in English the adjective always comes first, so "an old friend" is ambiguous. In Italian you must choose: someone you have known for years is *un vecchio amico*; a friend who is old is *un amico anziano* or *un amico vecchio*.

Examples:
- *Luca è un vecchio amico: ci conosciamo dalle elementari.* (Luca is an old friend: we've known each other since primary school.)
- *Quel povero ragazzo ha perso il lavoro.* (That poor boy has lost his job.)
- *Ho letto diversi libri su questo argomento.* (I've read several books on this subject.)

grammarPoints.title: Literary and bureaucratic forms: egli, esso, codesto, vendesi
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** novels, history books, laws and official notices use forms you will rarely hear in conversation. You mostly need to recognise them, and to use a few in formal writing.

Subject pronouns (the word for who does the action) of written Italian:

| meaning | literary / formal | everyday |
|---|---|---|
| he, she | *egli, ella* | *lui, lei* |
| it (thing, animal) | *esso, essa* | usually left out |
| they | *essi, esse* | *loro* |

- *egli* and *ella* are only for people and only as subjects; *ella* is now very old-fashioned.
- *esso* and *essa* are mainly for things and animals; *essi* and *esse* are used for people as well as things: *Il regolamento è stato approvato: esso entrerà in vigore a gennaio.*

Demonstratives (words like "this", "that"):
- *codesto* means "that, near you". Outside Tuscany it survives in official letters: *codesto Ufficio* (your office).
- *costui, costei* (this man, this woman), often with a scornful tone: *Chi è costui?*
- *colui, colei* (the one), mostly in *colui che* (he who), *colei che* (she who).
- *coloro che* (those who): *Coloro che desiderano partecipare...*

Bureaucratic words: *suddetto* (above-mentioned), *medesimo* (same), *il sottoscritto* (the undersigned).

Signs and ads attach *si* to the end of the verb: *vendesi* (for sale), *affittasi* (to let), *cercasi* (wanted).

**Watch out:** do not use *egli* or *esso* in speech or in an informal email: it sounds like a nineteenth-century novel. Say *lui*, or simply leave the subject out.

Examples:
- *Dante nacque a Firenze nel 1265; egli fu esiliato nel 1302.* (Dante was born in Florence in 1265; he was exiled in 1302.)
- *Coloro che desiderano partecipare devono iscriversi entro venerdì.* (Those who wish to take part must register by Friday.)
- *Vendesi appartamento in centro.* (Flat for sale in the town centre.)

grammarPoints.title: The subjunctive in real usage: dropping che, indicative in speech
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** real Italian handles the subjunctive more flexibly than textbooks. In writing, *che* is often dropped while the subjunctive stays; in relaxed speech, the subjunctive is often replaced by the indicative. Knowing when each is acceptable is a sign of mastery.

Dropping *che*. After verbs of opinion, hope and fear (*credo, penso, spero, immagino, temo, mi auguro*) and after *pare, sembra, si dice*, the *che* can be left out. The subjunctive stays:
- *Credo sia meglio partire presto.* (I think it's better to leave early.)
- *Spero tu stia bene.* (I hope you're well.)
- *Pare abbia vinto la lotteria.* (Apparently he won the lottery.)

Because *io, tu, lui* share the same present subjunctive forms (*abbia, sia*), add the subject pronoun when it isn't clear: *Penso tu abbia ragione.*

Indicative in speech. In conversation, many speakers say *Penso che è vero* or *Non so se viene*. In indirect questions this is widely accepted; after *penso che* it still sounds careless in writing. Keep the subjunctive in anything formal.

Where the indicative is the rule, not a shortcut:
- after verbs of certainty or knowledge: *So che hai ragione.* *Ho saputo che si è sposata.*

Where the subjunctive never drops, even in speech:
- after conjunctions such as *benché, prima che, affinché, senza che*: *Benché piovesse, uscimmo.*

**Watch out:** dropping *che* does not mean dropping the subjunctive. *Credo è meglio* is wrong; it is *Credo sia meglio* or *Credo che sia meglio*.

Examples:
- *Immagino siate stanchi dopo il viaggio.* (I imagine you're tired after the journey.)
- *Mi auguro vada tutto bene.* (I hope everything goes well.)
- *So che tu hai ragione.* (I know you're right.)

grammarPoints.title: Truncation and elision: buon, signor, gran, pur
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Italian often shortens words before another word. Truncation (dropping the last vowel or syllable) uses no apostrophe; elision (dropping a vowel before another vowel) uses one.

Truncation, no apostrophe:
- *buono* becomes *buon* before a masculine singular noun: *buon amico, buon giorno* (but *buono studente*, before s + consonant or z).
- Titles before a name: *signore, dottore, professore, ingegnere* become *signor Rossi, dottor Bianchi, professor Neri*.
- *grande* can become *gran*: *gran parte, un gran piacere*.
- *santo* becomes *San* before a consonant: *San Marco* (but *Santo Stefano*, before s + consonant).
- *bene* becomes *ben*: *ben fatto*; *pure* becomes *pur*: *pur sapendo* (even though he knew).
- *quale* becomes *qual*: *qual è* (no apostrophe).
- Infinitives in fixed phrases and poetry: *far vedere, aver paura, esser felice*.

Elision, with apostrophe, before a vowel:
- *santo*: *Sant'Antonio*; *grande*: *grand'uomo*; *bello*: *bell'aspetto*.
- *come è, dove è*: *com'è, dov'è*.

One exception to learn: *poco* becomes *po'* with an apostrophe, because a syllable is cut off: *un po' di pane*.

**Watch out:** *qual è* never has an apostrophe, because *qual* also exists before consonants (*qual buon vento*). *Qual'è* is a classic mistake, even among Italians. And keep the full form of a title when you speak to someone without their surname: *Buongiorno, signore!*, *Sì, dottore.*

Examples:
- *Buongiorno, signor Rossi!* (Good morning, Mr Rossi!)
- *Qual è il tuo colore preferito?* (What's your favourite colour?)
- *Pur sapendo la verità, non ha detto nulla.* (Even though he knew the truth, he said nothing.)
- *Vorrei un po' di zucchero.* (I'd like a little sugar.)

grammarPoints.title: Marked word order: inversion and focus
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Italian word order is flexible: the new or most important information usually goes at the end of the sentence. So the subject (who or what does the action) often comes after the verb, and putting a word first can make it stand out.

Subject after the verb:
- When the subject is the new information, especially with verbs of happening and arriving: *È arrivato il treno.* (The train has arrived.) *È successo un incidente.* *Mancano tre giorni.*
- To answer "who?": *Chi paga? Pago io.* (I'll pay.) *L'ho fatto io.* (I did it.) Also in the fixed *Lo dicevo io!* (I told you so!)
- In questions with a question word: *Dove sono andati i ragazzi?*

Putting a word first for emphasis:
- Contrast in speech: *Domani parto, non oggi!* (said with stress on *domani*).
- Literary and journalistic inversion: *Grande fu la sorpresa.* (Great was the surprise.) *Molto si è discusso di questa riforma.* (Much has been said about this reform.)

The neutral order is still subject, verb, object: *Marco ha chiamato.* The marked order tells the listener what matters: *Ha chiamato Marco* answers "who called?".

**Watch out:** English stresses a word with the voice ("*I* did it"); Italian moves it to the end: *L'ho fatto io*, not *Io l'ho fatto* (which does not sound like an answer to "who did it?"). And with a question word, do not keep the English order: *Dove sono andati i ragazzi?*, not *Dove i ragazzi sono andati?*

Examples:
- *Non preoccuparti, pago io.* (Don't worry, I'll pay.)
- *Mentre cenavamo, è arrivato Luca.* (While we were having dinner, Luca arrived.)
- *Grande fu la sorpresa quando lo vidi entrare.* (Great was my surprise when I saw him come in.)

grammarPoints.title: Pronoun idioms: smetterla, avercela con, farla franca
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** many everyday idioms are verbs with fixed pronouns attached (*la, ci, ne, si*), whose meaning you cannot guess from the parts. Learn them as whole words, with their conjugation.

| infinitive | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *smetterla* | to stop it | *Smettila!* |
| *avercela con* | to be angry with | *Ce l'hai con me?* |
| *farla franca* | to get away with it | *L'ha fatta franca.* |
| *cavarsela* | to get by, cope | *Me la cavo.* |

More you will hear every day:
- *prendersela* (to take offence): *Non te la prendere.*
- *sentirsela* (to feel up to): *Non me la sento.*
- *passarsela* (to be getting on): *Come te la passi?*
- *entrarci* (to have to do with): *Che c'entra?*
- *fregarsene* (colloquial: not to care at all): *Se ne frega.*
- *farcela* and *andarsene*, which you already know: *Ce l'ho fatta. Me ne vado.*

How they work:
- The reflexive pronoun changes with the person (*mi, ti, si, ci, vi*) and becomes *me, te, se, ce, ve* before *la* or *ne*: *me la cavo, te la cavi, se la cava...*
- In compound tenses the participle agrees with *la*: *ce l'ho fatta*, *se l'è presa*, *l'hanno fatta franca*.
- In the imperative the pronouns attach: *Smettila!*, *Smettetela!*; in the negative, both orders work: *Non te la prendere* or *Non prendertela*.

**Watch out:** do not drop the pronouns. *Ho fatto* means "I did"; *ce l'ho fatta* means "I made it". And use feminine *fatta, presa*, not *fatto, preso*, because the hidden *la* is feminine.

Examples:
- *Smettila di fare rumore!* (Stop making noise!)
- *Perché ce l'hai con me?* (Why are you angry with me?)
- *Non parlo bene il tedesco, ma me la cavo.* (I don't speak German well, but I get by.)
- *Il ladro l'ha fatta franca.* (The thief got away with it.)

grammarPoints.title: Tenses for style: historic present, narrative and polite imperfect
grammarPoints.noteMd:
**In short:** Italian tenses do more than place events in time. Writers and speakers choose them for effect: to make a story vivid, to sound polite, or to concede a point.

- **Historic present** (the present for past events): in history books and in lively storytelling. *Nel 1492 Colombo arriva in America.* *Ieri entro in un bar e chi vedo? Il mio professore!*
- **Historic future**: in a past narrative, the future for what happened later. *Dante non tornerà mai a Firenze e morirà a Ravenna nel 1321.*
- **Narrative imperfect**: in news reports, the imperfect for single completed events, to give a "live" effect. *Pochi minuti dopo, la polizia arrestava i rapinatori.* In ordinary speech you would use the passato prossimo.
- **Polite imperfect**: in shops and requests, the imperfect softens what you want. *Volevo un chilo di pane.* *Cercavo un paio di scarpe.* It means "I'd like", not "I wanted".
- **Play imperfect**: children set up a game with it. *Facciamo che io ero il re.* (Let's pretend I'm the king.)
- **Concessive future**: the future admits a point before a "but". *Sarà anche bravo, ma è antipatico.* (He may well be good, but he's unpleasant.)

**Watch out:** *Volevo un caffè* in a bar is not about the past, and the barista will simply serve you. Don't translate it as "I wanted". And the narrative imperfect is a written style: in conversation, say *Il ministro si è dimesso*, not *si dimetteva*.

Examples:
- *Buongiorno, volevo un chilo di pane.* (Good morning, I'd like a kilo of bread.)
- *Nel 1492 Colombo arriva in America.* (In 1492 Columbus reaches America.)
- *Il giorno dopo, il ministro rassegnava le dimissioni.* (The next day, the minister handed in his resignation.)
- *Avrà anche ragione, ma non doveva urlare così.* (He may well be right, but he shouldn't have shouted like that.)
